reviewText: "London Town" is a fairly spotty Wings album. Following their triumphant rock stadium tour of the United States, they kind of ran out of steam. The album does have its high points. The title song is a good atmospheric opener, and hints at some kind of musical grandeur, as does the poignant "I'm Carrying." "With a Little Luck" is a nice positive hit, and "Girlfriend" is a soppy classic. "Famous Groupies" is a fun upbeat one too, as is the Elvis pastiche "Name and Address." Unfortunately, some of the rest of these numbers are pretty dreary. Denny Laine is a good singer but neither of the songs he wrote here are worth much - if anything, they're even more lightweight than McCartney's worst, which isn't good. A lot of the lyrics are forced in songs like "Cafe on the Left Bank" and the silly "Morse Moose and Grey Goose." "Cuff Link" is a forgettable throwaway that anyone else would have left off an album. I'm pleased that the CD comes with bonus tracks, so that the famous hit single "Mull of Kintyre" can be heard again. I've never been sure why it was so popular, but it's catchy enough.

reviewText: I just received this remastered classic from Amazon and it is ASTOUNDING ! I can't believe it took me so long to pick this up. Miles sounds as good as I've ever heard him and the rest of the musicians are also at their best particularly Milt Jackson on the title track.  Monk sounds a bit tentative and the story is that Miles asked him to sit out while he took his solo but Monk came through when it was his time to comp behind Jackson's solo and take his own solo. He sounds inventive and unmistakably Monk. Horace Silver and Sonny Rollins both sound wonderful and the tracks where they are featured really swing. The heart of this fine CD is the incredible rhythm section of Percy Heath and Keny Clarke. These guys were rock solid throughout this session and with the remastering Heath's bass lines just jump through the speakers.Do not hesitate to purchase this. You will be glad you did.

reviewText: 50 Cent unquestionably had the biggest year of his career in 2003 with a breakout national debut in "Get Rich Or Die Tryin" under the wings of Dr. Dre and Eminem. Much like many other rappers, he is using his name to give some shine to a couple of the other names in his camp. 50 is bringing all of his G-Unit soldiers with him on this group album.G-Unit consists of 50, Lloyd Banks, the incarcerated Tony Yayo, and the new Southern representative Young Buck. 50 Cent, who just dropped an album a little more than a half a year ago seems tired and unispired on most of the tracks here. Clearly he didn't learn from rival Ja Rule that "overexposure" can be dangerous. Lloyd Banks who has been killing mixtapes with some of the hottest punchlines this side of Jadakiss also seems to be lost for new material. Tony Yayo, who is currently serving time only shows up on two tracks. 50's declaration that he felt that there was enough material from Tony to go forward with the album seems like a bit of a half truth used to cover up the fact that they wanted to push this LP as soon as possible. Young Buck who really never seemed to be that impressive in the early stages is actually the only who manages to bring his "A" game to the table.The first single, "Stunt 101" is a pretty average track to be a lead-off single but it does grow on you. The two Dre-produced joints, "Poppin' Them Thangs" and "G'd Up" are phenominal but this album could have used a little bit more help from the Good Doctor in the production department. Eminem is nowhere to be found on this release (aside from in the "Thank You" section of the linear notes). Perhaps this was a conscious decision by the group to show that they don't need the guaranteed sales that would come from him dropping a verse on this album. Unfortunately, his abscene is very noticeable.The biggest problem with "Beg For Mercy" is that it dabbles far too much in familiar territory. The Lloyd Banks solo, "Smile", while one of the album's biggest highlights, shares a similar theme and beat with that of 50's "21 Questions". The same can be said of the title track with its beat that sounds like a dead ringer for "Back Down". Tracks like "Baby U Got", "Groupie Love", and "I'm So Hood" get tired real fast with their repeative hooks."Beg For Mercy" should have been an excellent album but unfortuantely it seems that the G-Unit crew used up their best material on the mixtape circut. The production was satisfactory. Having so many tracks dedicated to females but only one track with a female chorus ("G-Unit") gave the album an uneven feeling. The content gets boring quick. There's only so many times that you can hear 50 singing hooks about groupies until you want to hit the "STOP" button on your CD player.

reviewText: Después de 3 excelentes discos (First-Horizontal-Idea, sin considerar los 2 australianos), los Bee Gees alcanzan su madurez y su punto máximo de creatividad en 1969 con Odessa. En medio de problemas internos que terminarían luego en una breve separación, los hermanos Gibb, Barry con 22 años y Maurice y Robin con sólo 19, entregan en este disco grandes temas con una densidad y orquestación pocas veces escuchadas antes. Pese a ser un álbum doble alcanzó el puesto 20 en EE.UU. y el 10 en Inglaterra, transformándose en el último éxito de su etapa "clásica" (1969-1973). Entre las canciones la más destacada es Odessa, que con siete minutos y medio demostró que ellos también podían hacer largos y elaborados temas sin caer en la monotonía. Resaltan tambien Melody Fair, I Laugh In Your Face y Never Say Never Again, aunque en realidad casi todas las canciones aportan, tal vez los 3 temas instrumentales sean excesivos, pero al mismo tiempo le dan a Odessa ese toque monumental que el tiempo se ha encargado de reforzar. No sólo el mejor trabajo de los Bee Gees, sino uno de los mejores del Pop de los años 60's.
summary: La obra maestra de los Bee Gees, y es 1969.

reviewText: Nothing But The Best is a Frank Sinatra album of just some of his best; this really can't be called a "best of" album because it has a mere twenty-two songs on it--and The Chairman certainly had more than twenty-two hits on any of his record labels! However, Frank's fans will love this album anyway; it does contain a few extra seconds here and there to capture Frank's comments. There is a very fine USPS commemorative stamp and, just as they say, there's a previously unissued rendition of "Body And Soul."The CD starts off with Frank Sinatra performing "Come Fly With Me." "Come Fly With Me" is the perfect upbeat start to this album; and Frank's voice is in excellent form. The big band style arrangement works well for this number and it whets your appetite for more--great! Similarly, "The Way You Look Tonight" has Frank again singing at his best with a more mature voice; but yet he uses this opportunity to showcase the magnificent qualities of his voice. Frank's excellent diction and his uncanny sense of timing enhance his singing even more.Frank gives "The Good Life" a very fine treatment and the music that accompanies him is very pretty but they never drown out Frank as he sings this very well. "The Girl From Ipanema" retains its usually bossa nova treatment but when Frank sings this you'll swear nobody could ever have sung this as well as Frank did! Frank takes ballads and puts his own stamp on them with his sublime interpretations of them; and this impresses me greatly."Strangers In The Night" sounds fresh and new when Frank sings this so very well; and the strings are used to great advantage. I love it! "Call Me Irresponsible" shines equally bright when Frank performs this with sensitivity; his voice remains in excellent form and it's truly a pleasure to hear him sing."That's Life" is actually one of my personal favorites on this CD (believe it or not); and Frank sings this with passion and all his might. The chorus that backs up Frank enhances the beauty of the number even further. Of course, "My Way" is a classic Sinatra tune; and I always love it when I hear Frank sing this. "My Way" is easily a major highlight of this album and I predict you'll enjoy this version of "My Way," too.The theme from New York, New York gets the royal treatment from Frank Sinatra--he was born to sing songs like this! WOW! The CD also ends nicely with Frank Sinatra performing "Body And Soul;" this previously unissued interpretation of this ballad is worth the price of admission alone!Sure, this CD contains just some of Frank's best from his later years; but I have a feeling many of his fans may want this after all. This is also a possible starter CD for newcomers to Frank's artistry and people who enjoy classic pop vocals will enjoy this as well.
summary: certainly not all of Frank's best--but it's still all right by me !!!

"Come Fly With Me" is the perfect upbeat start to this album; and Frank's voice is in excellent form. The big band style arrangement works well for this number and it whets your appetite for more--great! Similarly, "The Way You Look Tonight" has Frank again singing at his best with a more mature voice; but yet he uses this opportunity to showcase the magnificent qualities of his voice. Frank's excellent diction and his uncanny sense of timing enhance his singing even more.Frank gives "The Good Life" a very fine treatment and the music that accompanies him is very pretty but they never drown out Frank as he sings this very well. "The Girl From Ipanema" retains its usually bossa nova treatment but when Frank sings this you'll swear nobody could ever have sung this as well as Frank did! Frank takes ballads and puts his own stamp on them with his sublime interpretations of them; and this impresses me greatly."Strangers In The Night" sounds fresh and new when Frank sings this so very well; and the strings are used to great advantage. I love it! "Call Me Irresponsible" shines equally bright when Frank performs this with sensitivity; his voice remains in excellent form and it's truly a pleasure to hear him sing."That's Life" is actually one of my personal favorites on this CD (believe it or not); and Frank sings this with passion and all his might. The chorus that backs up Frank enhances the beauty of the number even further. Of course, "My Way" is a classic Sinatra tune; and I always love it when I hear Frank sing this. "My Way" is easily a major highlight of this album and I predict you'll enjoy this version of "My Way," too.The theme from New York, New York gets the royal treatment from Frank Sinatra--he was born to sing songs like this! The CD also ends nicely with Frank Sinatra performing "Body And Soul;" this previously unissued interpretation of this ballad is worth the price of admission alone!Sure, this CD contains just some of Frank's best from his later years; but I have a feeling many of his fans may want this after all. This is also a possible starter CD for newcomers to Frank's artistry and people who enjoy classic pop vocals will enjoy this as well.

reviewText: Bob Boilen has been raving about this album for a while, and I'm sure every other independent music spokesman has been too. Bon Iver is comprised mainly of Justin Vernon who isolated himself in a cabin in Wisconsin where he wrote this album over the course of a winter. The name Bon Iver is a pun on the French "Bon Hiver" which translates "Good Winter." The music is dark, haunting and entrancing and Vernon's vocals are so unique. The album is decorated with atmospheric harmonies, baritone guitars, twanging sounds, a dash of horns, and masterful production that brings out all of the different colors of winter. Grays, whites, blacks and the like. The lyrics are dark and pensive, and quite obscure. This album will be talked about for a while, since it's clear that something is holding it together as a cohesive unit but quite unclear what it is that is holding it together. I can't wait to drive in light snow with this album on the speakers and see where I end up. Whether you know what he's singing about, Bon Iver is certainly the perfect soundtrack to a bon hiver and this will probably find it's way close to the top of a lot of top albums lists at the end of the year.

reviewText: Karyn White was most popular in the late `80s.  Some of her contemporaries included Pebbles, Jody Watley and Paula Abdul.  Karyn probably received the least success of the three, but, ironically, I feel that she's the most talented.  She has a great vocal range and impressive control of her voice.  She is best known for her mega-hit, "Superwoman."  I really enjoyed all of her music which used to get a decent amount of airplay, and I wanted a closer look at her, so I listened to "Make Him Do Right."  I really enjoyed it!  This is Karyn's third album and it is great all across the board (production-wise, lyrically and vocally.)  Jimmy Jam and her former husband, Terry Lewis produced this album, and Babyface also stepped up to compose a few numbers.There are few up-tempo tracks on "Make Him Do Right", but that is alright with me because I love ballads and mid-tempos.  The few up-tempos on this album are the weakest on the album, and Karyn sounds akin to Shanice on her upbeat tracks.  That is a huge compliment because Shanice is an extraordinary, yet unsung, vocalist.  "Hungah", "Weakness" and "Simple Pleasures" are the only fast songs, but they don't make the album.  It's the slower numbers that capitalizes her vocal talent on, and I enjoy every minute.  "Can I Stay With You?" is such a masterpiece! This song is so sensual, yet very tasteful.  Karyn's voice sparkles like a rhinestone bra!  It's the albums strongest cut. "I'm Your Woman" and "Make Him Do Right" have memorable lyrics.  "I'm Your Woman" is about being delighted to be in a good relationship with a certain gentleman.  Also worth mentioning is the production and hook on this track, simply lovely they both are!  "Make Him Do Right" is another anthem for the ladies, just as "Superwoman" was.  This song is about not settling for less than great treatment from your object of affection.If you are into an R&B; diva with great vocals, true and well-written lyrics, and an undeniable sincerity in her voice, pick this album up today! Karyn, please come back to the music business and show some of these little girls how to really sing!  You are unforgettable, and that is why I'm writing a review for your album, which was released in 1994.Mikeisha's Top 51. "Can I Stay With You?"2. "I'm Your Woman"3. "I'd Rather Be Alone"4. "Nobody But My Baby"5. "Make Him Do Right"

reviewText: This 2004 album by Elton John contains mainly slow to medium tempo songs , and features an American country / ballad style on most songs. Having listened to just about every commercially-released Elton song on his multitude of past LP's and Cd's , I am pleased how Elton seems to be steering his musical career, and I do like Peachtree road more than I was expecting to (given the rather mixed reviews).I think Elton sounds great here. I really like his American South styled vocals on numbers like Porch Swing in Tupelo, and the laid-back country of Turn The Lights Out When You Leave. Piano-playing Elton is in fine voice on I Stop And I Breathe, and especially the impressive It's Getting Dark In Here ( one of lyricist Bernie Taupin's better recent compositions).But I love it when Elton sings inspirational, happy songs, which is why I really enjoyed the positive vibes of All That I'm Allowed and Answer In The Sky. My Elusive Drug is probably the best song here though - it is about triumph over demons and personal problems and Elton sings this really well. They Call Her The Cat is the only boppy song here, and although fun it's hardly essential . Elton certainly seems much better suited to soulful ballads than bar-room rockers these days , and now that the Weight Of The (commercial) World is off his back, he can enjoy a hopefully long spell as a relaxed "elder-statesman" of popular song.Long-time fans like me can be content with this enjoyable album for the next few years while he's playing shows in Vegas !!!

reviewText: This is the key Nick Drake album to get, with its excellent production values, and fully realized arrangements.  He's in great voice, and each song gets a sensitive treatment, whether its sonorous strings, or a bopping horn section, or a quiet bluesy piano.  The sax on At the Chime of a City Clock it is worth the price of admission.  Sad he couldn't hold it together enough to make more music--sad he died so young, but many in his era's British folk scene suffered, too.  This album is haunting AND optimistic--just listen to Hazy Jane II.  A classic which creates a mood from the first to the last track.

reviewText: The Staple Singers had been a together for nearly two decades when they landed at Stax in 1968. They'd recorded old-school spirituals for Vee Jay and folk-influenced sides for Riverside before finding a new direction with the Memphis soul powerhouse; not only did the Staples adapt to the soul and funk energy of Stax, but they evolved their material from the pointed social topics of the folk era to less specific, but highly empowering "message music." Their first two Stax albums, 1968'sSoul Folk in Actionand 1970'sWe'll Get Over, featured backing from the label's house band, Booker T. & the M.G.'s, and mixed terrific material from Stax songwriters with Staples' originals. Despite the quality of each release, nothing clicked on the charts, and the group's third long-player, 1971'sStaple Swingers, found Stax executive Al Bell taking over production chores from M.G.'s guitarist Steve Cropper.Even more importantly, Bell began recording the Staples' backing sessions in Alabama with the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section: Eddie Hinton (lead guitar), Jimmy Johnson (rhythm guitar), David Hood (bass), Barry Beckett (keyboards) and Roger Hawkins (drums). Hood's deep bass lines and Hawkins' rhythm touch anchor this album, solidified by Johnson's chords, Beckett's vamping and Hinton's inventive fills; the Memphis horns add texture and accents without ever needing to step out front to announce themselves. Produced at a time that Stax was evolving from its soul glories of the `60s to its funkier output of the early `70s, the Staples hit a third gear as they built the album's tracks, particularly the hit singles "I'll Take You There" and "Respect Yourself," from perfectly intertwined strands of soul, funk, and gospel. Also blended in to "I'll Take You There," as Rob Bowman astutely observes in the liner notes, is the reggae of the Harry J All-Stars' instrumental "The Liquidator."The album's original ten tracks include longer versions of the singles, stretching each to nearly five minutes. You can understand why the extra vocalizing of "Respect Yourself" was trimmed for radio play, but Staples fans will treasure the full-length production. Concord's 2011 reissue adds two previously unreleased bonus tracks: the cautionary "Walking in Water Over Our Head" and an alternate take of Jeff Barry and Bobby Bloom's "Heavy Makes You Happy." The latter forgoes the horn arrangement of the original single, emphasizes the rhythm section (as did all of engineer Terry Manning's album mixes), and adds forty-three seconds to the running time. These are great additions to an album that's already the best full-length of the Staples' career, and one of the best Stax ever produced. [2011 hyperbolium dot com]

reviewText: Although I wasn't around for the real Motown, I was raised on a steady diet of Phil Spector, Berry Gordy, Stax, Volt, Muscle Shoals, and Chicago and Delta Blues, so "Back to Black" immediately struck a chord. I've followed the careers of several neo-soul artists such as Ricky Fante, Joss Stone, and Corinne Bailey Rae, so I was interested to see how Winehouse compared.From the opening bars of "Rehab," you could *almost* think you were in the heyday of Motown, from the Spectoresque "Wall of Sound" production (chimes, what reviewers described as "fat drums" and "grunting saxophones"), to the anachronistically saucy lyrics about drinking ("I didn't get much in class, but I know it don't come in a shot glass") and classic soul ("I'd rather be at home with Ray [Charles], there's nothing you can't teach me that I can't learn from Mr. [Donny] Hathaway").The odd tracks are the strongest Northern Soul offerings. Track Three is the biting doo-wop ode "Me and Mr. Jones," with the intriguing intro of "What kind of f**kery is this? You made me miss the Slick Rick gig." Some of Amy's strongest, most assertive vocals are on Me and Mr. Jones."Back to Black" (Track 5) sounds like a lost Funk Brothers / Supremes track, with prowling piano bassline and bright tambourine that morph into a string-drenched chorus punctuated by chimes. The ghostly choir and stretch of silence mid-song punctuated only by tambourine beats make Back to Black a powerful, haunting declaration of loss and one of the most powerful soul songs of the last decade.Finally, the oft-discussed "Tears Dry On Their Own," a "Ain't No Mountain High Enough"- inspired anthem. This may be the most prominent example of the album's Motown roots, carefully and lovingly crafted. Except for the modern lyrics (" I f**k myself in the head with stupid men"), this sounds like it could have been an undiscovered gem from the Motown vaults. Amy's most soulful singing is unleashed on the chorus.The other tracks range from girl group / soul ballads ("Love Is a Losing Game," "Wake Up Alone," "He Can Only Hold Her," "Unholy War") to modern hip-hop (You Know I'm No Good, and a rap remix with Ghostface Killah as the bonus track). The only dud was the ska-heavy Just Friends, which I found grating and cloying after the excellence displayed on the above tracks. The American version substitutes the "You Know I'm No Good" remix in place of "Addicted," an ode to marijuana, a move which many fans denounced. I did not care at all for the rap remix, which felt like a last-minute move to appeal to rap fans rather than a well-thought-out bonus.Split between two producers (Salaam Remi and Mark Ronson), Back to Black pays fitting tribute to Amy's favorite artists, including the Shirelles, the Ronettes, and Carole King. Amy's tart, lewd lyrics offer up a shrewd look at dating and love in contemporary London and seem a natural counterpart to the 1960s soul and R&B; standards she channels. Perhaps her greatest accomplishment is making the Motown and Phil Spector sound her own - Back to Black always comes off as innovative and original rather than an attempt to imitate. If you love 1960s soul, Amy Winehouse's "Back to Black" feels like a long-lost friend.
summary: Sassy, slinky Winehouse pays tribute to Spector's girl groups and the Motown Sound

reviewText: For his  first american recordings Johnny Cash release Johnny Cash comes with a stripped down, sober, introspective and brilliant album. You wont here many rockabilly tunes on this one it's just the man in black with his  guitar and his voice. From the opening track Delia's gone where he tells a  comicallly violent story about his low down triflin' woman. It sets the  tone for the album that ranges from somber tracks like The beast in me and  thirteen to the introspective Why me lord, redemption to the humurous  Tennesee Stud and the man who wouldn't cry. It seems as though there is new  life coming out of him the material seems so fresh and johnny sounds better  than ever. A classic.

reviewText: This is one of my fave cds of all time.  I bout the cd in 2000, in London.  I only listened to ...& AND ON and BOOTY, just becuase they were funky.  But about 1 1/2 yrs ago I was like "lemme listen to this!" and now I've realized the power oif real and intuitive music.  Music from the soul cannot be denied.  To the casual listener the 70+ minutes of music may run together, but each song is so different so unique.  It begins with the ultra funky PENITENTIARY PHILOSOPHY, a good way to jumpstart this classic.  Next, is DIDN't CHA KNOW the minor hit that is as deep as the baseline.  LISTEN TO THE WORDS SHE SPEAKS THE TRUTH.  MY LIFE is funky and paints a picture of where Erykah is in her life.  ...& ON is good and I love the rap in the middle.  It is probably the one song that prob doesn't belong, no where near as good as the original ON AND ON.  But still good.  CLEVA shows that Erykah may not be the most beautiful or talented woman, but she is still cleva and is a very powerful song despite its uptempo beat.  HEY SUGAH is an interlude.  BOOTY is funky and is almost an extension of CLEVA, she is tellin a woman for example, "You may have your PHD, but he is still fine wit me and my GED." Number 8 is where this cd goes into high gear.  KISS ME ON MY NECK sets the tone for the rest of the cd, badu compares her mind to a flourishing garden and says whatever man steps her way must have water to water the flowers growing out of her mind.  DEEP STUFF!  A.D. 2000 is a ode to the man who was shot 41 times by NYC police in 2000.  It is a slow song, but says when she was gone you won't name buildings after me so they can exist in dilapidation.  Number 10 is one of my FAVES, ORANGE MOON is so beautiful.  Everytime I see and orange moon I think of this song.  It's so nice and its actually about how her son (Seven) is a reflection of her light, which makes him an orange moon.  Poetry in song!  IN LOVE WITH YOU is a duet with Stephen Marley, this song took some time to grow on me, but is very sweet and is a real love song.  No "hittin it from the back", no "freak-a-leak", but instead 2 people repeatin, "I'm in love with you" take a listen more powerful than you think.  At first I was dissapointed that BAG LADY was not the same as the video and radio, but then towards the end of the song when the breakdown begins her choruses repeat and repeat but then I realized that she wants to drill the idea into your head!!! Number 13 TIMES A WASTIN is nice and has a great message, but it just doesn't compare to the reason why this album is what it is.  GREEN EYES!!  GREEN EYES!!  It is a 10 minute song divided into three movements. The ultimate break up song. No, "I hate you get your shit", not even "Tyrone-esque". The first movement Badu claims that her eyes are green because she eats a lot of vegetables and not becasue her ex is with another woman.  The second movement shows a stronger Badu procalaiming her position.  She is saying that he missed out on it, and she can do it all by herself.  Just when you think she is walkin on, 7 min into the song it starts a relapse.  She comes back to him and is sayin "c'mon we can make this work" , "I still love you."  This song is the epitome of the end of a relationship.  This song is so underrated and it pisses me off that music this good is overlooked, because Nelly's (who I don't care for) cd just came out.  This should have been album of the year and all that other stuff.  I highly recommend this cd to Baduizm and Worldwide Underground and even Her Live cd.  It is remarkable to hear music this good.  I love E. Badu I just hope that she can come back even harder, but I'm tellin you I discovered this cd bout a year late, but its never too late to discover good music!!

reviewText: So High, Refuge, It Don't Have to Change, Stay With You, and Used to Love U are the best on this album for me. I'm actually beginning to feel Number One, I Can Change, Alright, She Don't Have to Know (of course I would never behave this way, but the beat and the flow are both good). I DEFINTELY believe that Ordinary People is going to get PLAYED TO DEATH on the radio and join the status of overrated songs.  His voice is very nice, but it doesn't stand out from anyone else I've heard.  Whomever said he sounds like Carl Thomas was thinking the same thing I did when I first really listened to Ordinary People on the radio. However, I do find myself singing the songs as I'm walking or just doing other stuff.  It was also good to hear him playing the piano.  I have so much respect for true musicians (the piano is no easy task!) who do not simply rely on the mixing board and all of that fancy equipment.  If you can do more than just dance around a stage, you are good with me!  The piano accompaniment (sp?) to Used to Love U is so amazingly subtle that unless you know music, you'll pay it no attention. I used to play in a classical band, so I always look for the subtle things that can "make" a song. I had no idea he was on Ms. Hill's Everything is Everything.  Great song!I do agree that the album can be divided into two parts: the Hip-hop laced half and the Soul-laced half.  The first half is probably more hip hop-like with Kanye rapping and talking about male genitalia. The first half features the songs that are just enough to reach out to the MTV faithfuls. I am convinced that Kanye is the new Diddy: rapping in songs where he really doesn't belong and inappropriate and corny lyrics.I'm a soul person at heart, so this album is a good mix of soul and R&B; for me. Hopefully he will only continue to hone his talents and not go in the opposite direction and sell out. Oh, and I hope all of this praise doesn't jinx Legend...this album is good but before we put it on classic status, let him put out another album and prove himself a little more.BTW, just bought his live cd from [...]  I am a SUCKER for live albums!  As a matter of fact, I'm in NC, but I'm thinking of going home in April to MD to see him with Alicia Keys.BTW, I have edited this review about six times.  It just gets better and better for me.
summary: I'm feeling some songs...bought it today from Best Buy

reviewText: Some sections of the following review have been fictionalized for the reader's pleasure...Listen up folks!  This is the first album I ever purchased.  A few months earlier, I'd been given a copy of R.E.M.'s Fables of the Reconstruction, but Asia's self-titled debut was the first album (along with Boston's Third Stage) on which I actually spent my own hard-earned money.  It was the summer of 1986 and I was just another high school kid putting in hard time at my local Hardees as a "day porter".  Day porter was the job no one wanted because it combined unloading the supply truck at 5 AM, cooking fries or burgers during the lunch rush, and generally working with garbage.  Each afternoon, I came home reeking of grease and garbage, the way only a day porter can.  In return for all the sweeping, mopping, trashcan-emptying, and furtive groping at the hands of one of the cashiers, I received less than four bucks an hour.One evening shortly after my 16th birthday, I knifed through the balmy night air in my parents' white Reliant K on a clandestine mission to my local K-Mart.  My parents were not crazy about me spending the money I was earning at Hardees on trifles, so my mission to enhance my music collection had to be conducted in complete secrecy.  Once inside the K-Mart, I spent at least an hour contemplating the bewildering options at hand before settling on Asia's self-titled debut and Boston's Third Stage.New purchases in hand, I returned to my car, popped Asia in my cassette deck and headed out onto Bypass Road.  Unfortunately, at the first stoplight, the Reliant K sputtered out.  After 5 minutes of futilely turning the ignition, I gave the sled up for dead in the middle of the road and ran back to K-Mart where I called my parents from a pay phone.  I felt as though I were being punished for my wasteful spending habits.Back at the car 10 minutes later, I found a policeman giving it the once over.  He asked me if it was my car and I nodded in the affirmative.  The cop grabbed me by the nape of the neck and slammed my head against the Reliant's hood.  Blood gushing from my forehead like a young Jon Ritchie, I mustered up just enough strength to pull away briefly.  In return, I received a right uppercut to the jaw and a knee to the stomach that left me doubled over and gasping for breath.  Once I'd been properly subdued, the cop offered me several Hydrox cookies and a styrofoam cup of Diet Rite soda.  He went back to his patrol car and made a call.  When he returned, he was apologetic.  He said that I bore an unfortunate resemblance to a burglar wanted on the south side of town and that in "the heat of the moment", he had made a regrettable snap decision to beat me up and ask questions later.  In his "wildest dreams", he'd never imagined he would assault an innocent teenager and admitted that he was now "one step closer" to the suspension his supervisor had threatened him with a month earlier when he was the "sole survivor" of a showdown with a knife-wielding hobo.  For the sake of his wife and children's continued prosperity, I agreed to tell my parents that I'd incurred my injuries by tripping and falling into a patch of briars and brambles along the highway median.When my dad arrived, he was shocked by my bloody visage, though seemed to buy the briar patch excuse.  He quickly surmised that I'd simply flooded the Reliant by giving it too much gas and that it would soon be operational again.  He thanked the cop for looking out for me and before we knew it, we were headed back home.Pretty exciting story, isn't it?  If only Asia's self-titled debut was equally as exciting.  On a lark, I recently decided to purchase a used copy of the CD for sentimental purposes.  How does it sound 15 years after I bought that first copy on tape?  A whole lot cheesier than it used to, that's for sure.  I must admit the first cut, "Heat of the Moment", is still as rocking as ever, "Only Time Will Tell" remains irresistible, and "One Step Closer" and "Here Comes the Feeling" still have their charms.  Nevertheless, between the often wince-inducing lyrics and very 80s keyboard riffs, some of these songs are pretty embarrassing for me to be listening to here in the new millennium.  When was the last time you heard something as awful as "Time Again", which sounds like bad Boston, or "Wildest Dreams", which sounds like bad Rush?I'd have to conclude that Asia is worth pulling out for the occasional listen, but I can't say I've rediscovered a forgotten classic by any means.  It is a generally enjoyable piece of 80s pop rock and I guess there's something to be said for that.  Certainly a reasonable choice if you have a hankering for guitar-and-synth rock and feel reasonably confident you can get it home without suffering a beat-down at the hands of an overeager cop.

reviewText: First off, don't see my 3 stars and think badly of this recording. Rather than rate and compare one cd to all other cds I compare cds to other cd's by the same or similar artists. 5 stars being essential, 4 stars being great, and 3 stars being good with off-and-on greatness.To a certain extent I do consider this to be an essential recording because WISE ONE and LONNIE'S LAMENT are two of Coltrane's most affecting ballad melodies. As a whole album though I really cannot say that this is equal with the truly essential (from the first note to the last note) Coltrane recordings such as MEDITATIONS, SUN SHIP, etc...I guess what I am really saying is this... if you are looking to make your first Coltrane purchase I would point you to other cds before this one, but if you are an established fan of Coltrane then you need to add this cd to your collection, though only really for WISE ONE, LONNIE'S LAMENT, and THE DRUM THING.

reviewText: Teedra Moses - Complex Simplicity (TVT, 2004)This is a pretty solid album. Her potty mouth caught me off guard though (she curses in at least two songs, "You'll Never Find" and "You Better Tell Her"), but if you can get past that, you'll enjoy the album. My favorite is the very first one, "Be Your Girl", which is the current single, and the sexy "Backstroke". "Take Me" with Raphael Saadiq is also smooth and if you like that duet, check out Raphael's Ray Ray album where they do two duets. The album kinda drags in the middle and she reminds me so much of Amerie (and I don't know yet if that's a compliment), but it's still worth checking out. -EJR

reviewText: Baby makin music indeed! Joe is no stranger to serenading his listeners with smooth, sensual love songs. What makes this album different from his previous works is that he does it pretty much the entire album. One this I notice about this CD is that it is definitely paced slower then his past works, especially Joe Thomas New Man. To be blunt, this is a great album to set the mood (romantically of course), and could see a lot of spins throughout the night. But anyway, enough bedroom suggestions, back to the album!Overall, this isnt Joe's best, but its still pretty friggin good. Its still the same ol Joe that we know and love to listen to.Music production: 5/5. Very well done as usual. Joe usually picks his instrumentals well, so no surprise there.Content: 3/5. Like I said, this is a serenading album. This man his tryin to take somebody to bed with his music! That being said, the subject matter is pretty predictable and monotonous. He's saying the same thing to a different tune I guess. Its still good though.Lyrics: 4/5. Whether Joe writes his music or not, usually its done pretty well. This album is written pretty well, but it falls short on originality at times. With titles like "Sex Girl" and "I Wanna Be Your Lover" and "Miss My Baby", it suggests that there was a lack of effort in making this a lyrically rich project. But all that means is that you arent likely to be grabbing any quotable lines from good ol Joe this time around. It still sounds great though.Overall, the album gets  a solid 4/5. Worth my [...] bucks, and an great adition for all the romantics out there.

reviewText: HAHAHA!Sorry, but I couldn't resist.Yeah, I tend to go for Tobin's twisted landscapes, but nobody can do beauty, peacefullness, and beautiful bliss like Shadow.  This album is a landmark, and one of the quintessential albums of electronic music.  Of course, there are so many great albums, and that says quite a bit.  Even with today's superior electronics and, uh, Tobin (last time I compare him to Shadow), it still hasn't aged.  Of course, I wasn't aware of this album until last summer, but it sounds fresh as a spring morning. He is the master at beautiful collages, and if electronic music has soul, than  Shadow is the soul keeper (Lame, I know), the gatekeeper of beauty.Warm like a blanket, dark as night, cold and chilly, blissfull peace, there are so many moods.  There isn't any real tension in this album, as it doesn't have to.  Midnight In A Perfect World is perfect for the urban  bliss.  Stem/Long Stem is a stark, lonely, dark, myserious, with a hint of light.  Building Steam with A Grain Of Salt?  Rain, mesmerizing.  What Does Your Soul Look Like explore that your soul is multifaced.  It will truly conjure up something, maybe even exactly what you soul look likes (there are more of Soul Look Like songs onPreemptive Strike).  There's even some breaks, such as the untitled track, the more uptempo The Number Song (which is better than I once thought, for sure), and the best one yet, Why Hip Hop Sucks in 96', a great stab at the lame rap music at the time (I can't imagine what Why Hip Hop sucks in 08' sounds like).Shadow will prove to you that he is an artist.  Too many ________ electronic "artists" let everything do the work for them, set their machines on overdrive, and operate it like it a machine.  One little change, it's soul less, thoughtless, robotic.  Shadow takes samples, melds,  cuts, pastes, he's brilliant.  He uses tension, he uses his instrument as that, as he adds twists, turns, he's the master at that (certainly nearly on par as a certain Brazillian Born artist).  Besides, he's just pretty much using already recording material and just playing a bunch at the same time, on a ________ turntable and other stuff.  Not much different, if you really think about it.Add my voice to the numerous five star reviews.  It remains a cornerstone that all music lovers should purchase, no questions asked.10/10

reviewText: I had never bought a Tracy Chapman CD/LP/cassette in my life. I loved Fast Car ten years ago or so, but I hated Give Me A Reason (may not be exact title). But the moment I heard Telling Stories and downloaded the video on my RealPlayer, I thought maybe I'd take the plunge and buy my first Chapman CD. I loved the song, thought the video was weird. Maybe Tracy is better heard than seen! Anyway, I figured if I didn't like the CD, I'd always give it to somebody for Christmas! :) The first song, title cut, I was familiar with. What was to come? Wow. I ain't seen NOTHING YET!! I LOVE the "Africa" in that song! But I also find "First Try" very Oriental-sounding and beautiful. That's not even taking into account what a wonderful, capable guitarist this young lady is! I keep hearing reviews about dark and brooding songs, but  I'm sorry, I don't hear any of that. I guess you have to be a world-music lover like me to enjoy this. I'm enjoying the heck out of it, myself. This album is a winner on all counts as far as I'm concerned. There's not a bad song in the lot! My CD is not going to ANYBODY for Christmas! Maybe I'll send a tape, though. This was the best $... I'd spent so far this year (got mine at CDNow...)

reviewText: At it's best, rap can scour your cranium with red-hot lyrics and blistering beats.  It can raise political awareness, yet also provide the perfect soundtrack for a night out.  Some artists are able to handle this dichotomy; 2Pac is a perfect example.  He was able to speak eloquently about social deterioration ("Keep Ya Head Up," "To Live and Die in LA") , while bragging about his sexual prowess ("I Get Around") and violent lifestyle ("California Love").<<Pain Is Love>> is truly the lowest rap can go.  Not content with perpetuating black gangsta stereotypes (the cleverly titled "Dial M for Murder"), or giving us perhaps the worst Stevie Wonder rip-off since "Gangsta's Paradise" (the absolutely mindless "Livin' It Up"), Ja Rule must also subject us to some of the degenerate singing imaginable (the beauty/beast 'duet' of "I'm Real).  From it's start (how many more Prince Paul-style skits do we need?)  to its end (an attempt at redemption that rings hollow in light of statements elsewhere on the album), <<Pain is Love>> highlights the decline of what used to be a potent and relevant art form.Like all other American creative art, rap has been put on the assembly line, packaged, and commercialised.  The media has long known the profitability of perpetuating stereotypes, so why would they stop here?

reviewText: Update- February 20, 2011I have to sincerely apologize for my extremely negative original review.  I originally didn't have a clue how to understand the many layers of complexity -not to mention the bands highly original and innovative sound- they utilized on their early 70's albums, so my point here is this- when I gave Can's Soundtracks a rating of 2 out of 5, to put it simply, I didn't GET the album (or the band for that matter).I'm playing it again tonight and OH MY GOODNESS!  How could I possibly not like "Mother Sky?"  I complain about the screechy guitar solo in my original review, which as I realize now was a GIGANTIC mistake because it's honestly not even remotely obnoxious.  I didn't get it at first- that's the problem.Anyway, a more accurate way of describing "Mother Sky" is that it starts off with a melodic, fast-paced guitar solo reminiscent of Roxy Music perhaps, then it shifts into a psychedelic and melodic vocal melody before the basslines get all groovy, then the guitar jam returns and resembles a solo from something on Tago Mago and over the course of 14 minutes, not *once* was I bored with this magnificent track.Seeing as how a 14-minute track is basically half of the albums length, it seems only fair to change my overall rating of Soundtracks from a 2 to a 4 based on "Mother Sky" alone.Now something else I said in my original review that was completely wrong is that "Tango Whiskeyman" is a poor mans Radiohead.  What?  I was WAY off with that logic.  It's actually a highly original-sounding pop song with a sound that Radiohead probably heard and took advantage of for their own style.  Considering something that sounds like *this* was released over 40 years ago, well, my mind is totally blown.  I bet even the Beatles -assuming they knew about Can- had to have been impressed and tipped their hats to a radically new sound not yet heard at that specific period in time.No, this album won't ruin the legacy of Can.  That was a stupid thing for me to say.  Maybe I was in a bad mood when I wrote my original review?  It's the only explanation for my many glaring mistakes.I should have mentioned a few other songs too.  "Deadlock" takes a guitar tone that can best be described as part screechy and part beautiful, and makes it VERY melodic by combining it with the vocal melody.  I can't explain how it works so well but I guess a little bit of creativity goes a long way.  "Soul Desert" has a GREAT groove- in fact, the entire song is based on that one simple groove, and it works.  Reminds me of the Rolling Stones hit "Hot Stuff".I still don't care for "She Brings the Rain" but who cares?  It's a 4 minute track on a 35 minute album.  I can easily dismiss it.Anyway, here's my original review which is NOT correct, but hey, I'll leave it here if for no other reason it definitely proves the music of Can takes time and dedication to adjust to it, and my original review is solid proof.  So have a blast reading and remember- I LIKE Soundtracks now.An album like this could potentially ruin the career of a legendary band like Can, haha.  Luckily this *is* just a soundtrack album after all.  Also it's not like this album went down as being an embarrassment for the band members.  The album just... faded away into obscurity.  Tago Mago is the album people should remember and purchase of course."Tango Whiskyman" is probably one of the better songs from Soundtracks, but it still pales in comparison to the majority of Monster Movie, for instance (or any one of the bands legitimate albums for that matter).  Some people believe this song resembles Radiohead, but let's be honest, Radiohead are much much better songwriters than this song represents.  This song just sounds like the lead singer mumbling along to the same exact notes as the guitar, and it's not even *good* guitar playing for that matter either."Don't Turn the Light On, Leave Me Alone" has a rather bland verse melody that doesn't seem to go anywhere, but some of the flute playing is rather nice.  Again, I can't understand the lead singer no matter HOW many times I play this track.  Ugh!I can't think of any reason to listen to a song like "Soul Desert" either.  Once again the lead singer isn't doing anything appealing with his vocal range except dragging it through the mud for an unnecessarily long period of time.  I will admit this song has a refreshing sound to it though.  Extremely weak songwriting completely rules over this album of course, but it *sounds* good at least."Mother Sky" features some of the noisiest and screechiest guitar playing I've ever heard.  It almost sounds like the beginning of Roxy Music's "Mother of Pearl" but a huge difference being Roxy Music was definitely MUCH better than pretty much everything featured from Soundtracks.  Talk about guitar playing that seriously doesn't need to be heard for any longer than 1 minute, let alone 14.  The vocals are pretty weak and unacceptable here as well."She Brings the Rain" features vocals that honestly make my stomach turn a little bit.  However, I will admit that the vocals are definitely an acquired taste.  You might love them.  However, the final 2 minutes at the end features a jam that sounds *very* dated and might remind someone of either Bread or Sugarloaf, but at least it's more tolerable than that verse melody (again, matter of taste).You know despite some horribly dated moments, it should be known other moments of the album show some distinct musical ideas that only a band like Can would be willing to attempt.  Such as on "Don't Turn the Light On, Leave Me Alone".  I may not *like* the song, but it definitely sounds different from most early 70's rock (perhaps mainly due to the lead singer).  The instrumental parts are definitely severely dated though.  However, any distinctive features are few and far between, so definitely do not expect an experimental outburst of musical ideas similar to Tago Mago.Let's just forget this album even exists, haha.  Like I said above, it's not like Soundtracks ruins the reputation of the otherwise experimental and creatively brilliant work of Can, because most people don't even remember it.  Good thing.

reviewText: Simply put, Waylon Jennings undoubtedly was the greatest outlaw cowboy singer that ever lived. His history, actually having been present and almost done in on "The Day the Music Died" when Buddy Holly, The Big Bopper and Richie Valens told Waylon, who had a cold, to take the bus is legendary and astoundingly prophetic. Afterwards, Buddy Holly's tinker toy plane ditched in the throes of a North Dakota Artic like night when crystal like ice permeated the atmosphere and contaminated their survival like a runaway cobra in a Bombay marketplace. Waylon went on to greatness and on this CD, songs like Mammas Don't let Your Babies Grow Up to be Cowboys, Are You Sure Hank Done it this Way and Luckenbach Texas are indescribably ingenious in their presentation and quality. You have Willie Nelson duets (Waylon and Willie) that are outstanding because to put it bluntly, Willie is no slouch either. Waylon, with his syrupy and very demanding and forceful vocals coupled with guitar finesse and his sheer presence as a man who has lived through it all, evolved subsequent to that fateful and disappointingly tragic day in the late fifties when those rock and roll fans who sensed that something affecting their futures like a bullet to the heart perceived that Waylon would be the scion to carry all of it on, realized that Waylon was not only country, he was iconic and unique to the point of an infinity-like fabric. My recommendation as a CD Reviewer of some prominence is for you to build a library of Waylon Jennings Cd's. Waylon was not only a pioneer, he was simply the best.Jay Adler  Massapequa, New York

reviewText: This album is good in that it tries to expand the big beat magic that made Dig Your Own Hole such a popular mainstream dance/electronica album, but it doesn't do it so well. The overall machine-like 1980s computer sounds on tracks like "Music: Response" and "Hey Boys, Hey Girls" decreases the worth of many of the tracks. There are some decent gems to be found here ("Out of Control" happens to be a personal favorite), but Come With Us is a better example of the Chems expanding that magic that is big beats.

reviewText: I've known about this band all along but somehow I've failed (miserably!) to feel their full impact until very recently, probably some sort of auditory ADD, or maybe there's just too much out there for me to keep up.  Listening to Travis' catalog and reading some of the other fans' great reviews, I'm not surprised by the comparisons to Radiohead, Coldplay and Keane. I could almost swear that Keane's Tom Chaplin's vocal cords were cloned from Fran Healy, whose beautiful, passionate vocals make this album really soar.  The truth is, comparisons are neither necessary nor particularly fair; Travis stands alone, with melodies that are pure magic, featuring a bright, vibrant guitar and powerful but not overpowering bass and rhythms. The production on this 1999 release reveals a band that clearly has a sense of their strengths and their musical mission.  Whether cranking it for the pleasure of having great music fill your world, or sitting in a dark room to contemplate the often touching lyrics, Travis fills the bill.  Two particular stand-outs for me are the pretty, plaintive, "Writing to Reach You," and "Why Does It Always Rain on Me," which may be the best representation of what this release has to offer throughout.  And somehow you just cannot help but feel for the guy's aching heart when he sings, "I can't sleep tonight/Everybody saying everything's alright/Still I can't close my eyes/...Where have you gone?/I get the strangest feeling you belong"  Well, one never knows, maybe the music will bring her back...

reviewText: Krall is smart, stylish and smooth.Her rich intelligent tones linger long after the song has ended and the stereo has been de-powered for another night.Her rhythmic reading of "I Remember You" is a case in point. It's a trite song with an even triter lyric but in the hands of Krall it becomes a memorable and evocative reflection of something lost but not forgotten.In a world post-Ella, post-Morgana, Krall's timing and nuance is a genuine joy to behold."Dancing in the Dark" - and its notions of romantic love - is again delivered with surety and great style. Its tender message is articulated with deliberation, timing and a soft emotion that never degenerates into the sentimental.On this wonderful five star affair, Krall's voice flows from the speakers with the reassuring and familiar tone of someone you know. Or wish you did.

reviewText: Indeed.  1980 was the year I graduated, and I can remember when this bad boy hit.  My cousin brought the album back from Philly where it was huge.  Diana?, bumpin' in the hood.  Well, yes courtesy of Chic who could do no wrong at that point.  The Chic mix is jazzier and features a more relaxed Diana.  Having grown up with the Motown mix, I think just the familiarity of it assures it's place as one of my favorites, that said I do prefer the Chic mixes of Friend to Friend, Tenderness, and Give Up.  Surprisingly, the Diana mix of Have Fun (Again), easily my fave track on the cd is a lot better than the Chic mix.  The guitar after the false ending gets me every time.  It also predicts the drum and bass groove in so many songs now.Disc 2 is kind of a let down, I mean can you really improve on the orignal Love Hangover?  10:00 min seems to be a little overkill.  The Supremes medley is blasphemy, the Stars on 45 ploy wears off very quickly.  The rest are pleasent but not essential listening.Thanks Universal for releasing the Chic Mix if only to illustrate the wisdom of Diana Ross and Motown and the daring of Chic to challenge her in a new direction.

reviewText: "Speak Now" is Taylor Swift's recent musical creation that is very original, creative, upbeat, and left me feeling very peaceful and content. You can really feel her happiness and enthusiasm through her singing in this collection such as in the musical numbers of "Mine" and "Enchanted". Most of the songs are very upbeat, but even the more solemn songs make you think such as "Haunted". Watching the music video to "Mine" compelled me to buy this collection because the song is both serious and happy at the same time.  The seriousness side is regarding the song's meaning where her and the person she falls in love with navigates the practical realities of life (where she sings about living together, and singing about paying the bills). The happy part is how the challenges of navigating this only brought them closer together (there is a part in the song where she sings about a fight at 230am, and just when she thought the relationship was over, he (the person she fell in love with) reassures her that he plans to stay with her even in spite of the challenges. This is why I say that "Mine" is a song that has a serious undertone, but is also happy and beautiful at the same time. Most of the songs on the cd are very good.  The only song that I have to admit that I must give more of a chance is "Last Kiss".  "Last Kiss" is ok, but is definitely a song that I would have to play more to enjoy (although there may be others reading this who are going to love "Last Kiss"). My favorite songs in this collection are "Enchanted", "Better Than Revenge", and "Sparks Fly". "Enchanted" is a very beautiful song about her developing intense feelings for someone that she connects to on a deep level who captivates her (hence her saying I was enchanted to meet you).  "Better Than Revenge" is a creative musical number about how people can be much more powerful and stronger than what they appear to be on the surface. Truthfully, Taylor does sing about taking revenge on another female that may have been unaware of her power and  more from an intent to give her a taste of her own medicine, (not from a physical or dangerous perspective). "Better Than Revenge" is a great musical pop, country, and rock hybrid (the guitar sounds used in the song are very enjoyable). However, my overall favorite song in this collection is the very happy, uplifting, and fun "Sparks Fly".  "Sparks Fly" is a fantastic song about how someone gives her the butterflies and a feeling of romantic excitement just from smiling at her. She sings this song so joyfully and passionately that you really get the sense of a happy soul singing about a person that makes her feel alive.  I say to definitely consider getting this collection if you like any of the following songs: "Teardrops on my Guitar", "Lovestory", and/or "Mine". Fortunately, she is going to perform in the area that I live the summer of 2011. I definitely intend to go to her concert

reviewText: DEVO do what they do best and I do thank you DEVO! Yes! This album is like a refreshing blast from the New Wave past and then some. It's hard to believe that it's been twenty years since DEVO last did an album together?! To tell you the truth, over the years I had given up hope and never thought they'd ever do another album again. But when I first heard that familiar DEVO sound on a famous Dell computer commercial a couple of years ago, well, I had an inkling of hope that maybe, just maybe something was coming down the pipe soon from my favorite New Wave band from the Eighties. And Lo and behold it has arrived.Contrary to popular belief, DEVO is not a one hit wonder. No Sirs and Madams. These guys came up with many hits over the years, and from what I am hearing on this new disk, they have done it once again. I am hearing hit after hit on this album with such great ditties as Sumthin', Fresh, Mind Games, Don't Shoot I'm a Man, Please Baby Please, What We Do...Heck, the whole album is a hit as far as I am concerned.So sit back, crank it up, put on your energy domes, and spazz out with these old school New Wave masters as they show you how it's really done the DEVO way.Standout Tracks are: ALL OF THEM!

reviewText: Having produced an album of aggressive spoken word, Gil Scott-Heron began moving into the direction he would spend his career.  Taking his political and social commentary from "Small Talk At 12th & Lenox" but this time backing it with jazz arrangements (accompanied by long-time collaborator Brian Jackson and a series of New York sessionmen), this album is probably the best of Scott-Heron's early work.Musically, its deep in a funky jazz vein, with an absolutely incomparable rhythm section of ROn Carter and "Pretty" Purdie holding down the groove.  Lyrically, Scott-Heron is looking on a bit smaller of a scale then he did on that previous album, while there's still some of that sort of far reaching social material (openers "The Revolution Will Not Be Televised", this time given a full arrangement and the achingly beautiful "Save the Children"), the majority of it is much more personal.  Nothing illustrates this more clearly than "Home is Where the Hatred Is", one of the most direct and honest assessments of drug addiction I've ever heard.  If you're ever known someone in the throwsof addiction, you'll realize just how painful this piece can be to listen to.  Ditto for "Pieces of a Man", a dark social commentary about people being unable to continue coping.  But what thing that separates this album from its predecessor in mood is there is more variety-- the thoroughly optimistic "I Think I'll Call It Morning" for example, and the ecstatic "Lady Day and John Coltrane".All in all, a fine jazz vocal record, recommended.
summary: The best of Scott-Heron's Flying Dutchman recordings.

reviewText: My first couple of listens to this album disappointed me. It wasn't what I expected, and the songs seemed so depressing. Anyway, recently I have started to listen to it more and have found it to be very relaxing and beautiful. I beg anyone who doesn't like it at first, to please give it a chance...it is worth it, and is a terrific cd to play during those quiet reflective moments we all have. Yes, it is a change of pace for Alison, but I think it's necessary for an artist to grow, and have changes every now and then. And I'm sure that we haven't heard the last of Alison Krauss and Union Station's own brand of bluegrass. They'll be back! But in the meantime, this album is here to enjoy.
summary: This album really does grow on you

reviewText: i am a huge fan of ronnie james dio.  i love dio's band (of the same name) as well as sabbath era dio.  in fact sabbath era dio beats ozzy's era hands down for me so i was curious about the band dio started in.  i was shocked.  this IS NOT metal or anything close to rainbow or sabbath era dio or dio, the band itself.  it is blues rock straight and simpel, in my opinion.gone is the range and brilliance that dio acheived in later bands.  there is no guitar magic.  there is little magic.  what magic there is comes in the way of heart.  this is a very emotional album but that is what good blues is all about.  i was a little disappointed.there are a couple of songs that are good and a few moments that rock but all in all this album is a 3 star middle of the road venture, neither dropping to the bottom nor rising to the stars of greatness.
summary: blues meets rock for little fire

reviewText: The time-frame in which this came out (late 1984) really was Hall & Oates at their peak.  Perhaps not musically, but certainly this came out at the very high point of their career.  They were on magazine covers, had their own HBO concert special ("The Liberty Concert" in 1985 - if you are a fan, check out the clips on Youtube).  Some people have said that this album finds H&O; "slipping" a bit, but I think it finds them in top form, and stands up next to just about anything they had done between 1980 and 1983.This album is the natural progression of where their sound had been going since 1980's "Voices" and through 1982's "H2O" and through to 1983's "Say It Isn't So" and "Adult Education" -- namely a big beat, pop-dance-oriented sound.  To add to the "big beat" sound Arthur Baker was brought in to remix the whole thing.  (For those who don't know, Arthur Baker was one of the top remixers/dance-music producers of the 1980's, working with, among others, New Order).The singles from this ("Out of Touch", "Method of Modern Love", Possession Obsession") are pretty representative of the sound of the album as a whole.  Perhaps the one downfall of this album is that, bringing in someone to remix all of the tracks did result in a bit of a sameness of the overall sound and feel of the tracks.  Also, as another reviewer stated, this thing is state-of-the-art 1984.  That means it definitely sounds of its time.  But, in my opinion, I have always really liked every song on this one.  It's hardly high art, but it is solid mid-80's pop music.If you are a casual fan looking to go a bit deeper with H&O; than a hits compilation, then this one isn't for you (get "Abandoned Luncheonette" and "Voices" instead).  But, if you are a more than just casual fan wondering if you should add this to your collection, I think you will be very happy with this one.  In my opinion, I don't think there is a bad song on this album.  A lot of 1980's "cheese" but, then again, that was really what the 1980's were about.I can tell you the 2004 remaster is obviously far better than the original pressing LP and cassette versions of this thing that I had in the 1980's.  But, I am not sure the 2004 remaster is that much ahead of the 1996 version (which I also owned).  I would recommend the 2004 remaster because it does have the original lyrics/liner notes, and some bonus tracks, including the remix of "Out of Touch" that was included on the original 1984 cassette (the 1996 version has neither).As for the songs, if you like "Out of Touch" and "Method of Modern Love" then you will like this album.2013 UPDATE -- I really cannot recommend the 2004 remaster anymore. Quite frankly, I think it's terrible (NOT the album proper, but the 2004 remaster).  Buy the original RCA Made in Japan CD, which sounds far superior. The music on this remaster is certainly "louder" but the tradeoff is that the music is clipped -- the crash of the cymbals, the curl of the bass, all those things that make for a great listening experience, are lost in exchange for a CD that doesn't require the volume to be turned up quite as loud.  The original RCA Made in Japan CD has far more detail to the music.  You can probably find it pretty cheap on eBay or a local used store.  Buy this for the bonus tracks; get the original RCA if you want to hear this album in all its glory.

reviewText: For those who know System of a Down from their self titled debut this album is an all love and respects due follw-up.System offer a rich, thick and unique blend of raw talent and fast paced passion. Taking an original spin on a metal-punk(even dare I say "carnival") fusion, System encourage thier listener to cast aside commercialism and purely enjoy what diffrences free-thinking can promote.System of A Down push the envelope of originality and remain a powerhouse for the future of rock music.

reviewText: Bun B is back with his first solo album in his 15 or so years in the game. For the past 4-5 years since Pimp C has been in jail (and UGK has been on a temporary hiatus), Bun B has made many guest apperances on albums from artists such as 8 Ball & MJG, Beanie Sigel, Big Tymers, DJ Kayslay Mike Jones, Paul Wall, Slim Thug, T.I. & more."We gon' run them ho's out and put some trill n****s in'Cause what happened in New Orleans should never happen again" The InaugurationFirst off, the production is handled by a handful of different people. Cory Mo ('The Inauguration'), KLC ('Bun'), Mr. Lee ('Get Throwed', 'Pushin' & 'I'm A G'), Salih ('Draped Up' & 'Draped Up Remix'), Mannie Fresh ('I'm Fresh' & 'What I Represent'), Lil Jon ('Trill Recognize Trill'), Jazze Pha ('I'm Ballin'), Bido ('The Story'), Trey Songz & Bei Major ('Hold U Down'), Mr. Collipark ('Git It'), Bigg Tyme ('Who Need A B'), Sean Wee ('Retaliation Is A Must'), and Travis Barker ('Late Night Creepin') of Blink-182 even contributes a track. The production on this album consists of top notch southern beats, while none of the beats are really innovative (besides maaybe 'The Inauguration'), every single one is dope in it's own way. As you can see from the production credits, there isn't just one type of southern production throughout the album either. Mr. Collipark drops a beat with the same feel as his other 2005 hits, 'Wait' & 'Play', while Lil Jon serves up a typical dope crunk beat for 'Trill Recognize Trill', and Bigg Tyme's beat on 'Who Need A B' combines the old school Oakland sound to compliment the Too Short guets apperance, and new millennium southern rap elements to help compliment Juvenile and Bun."It's Houston, Texas, motherf***er, you know the nameAnd we'll see you in February for the All-Star Game" Draped Up (Remix)As always, Bun B is on point lyrically throughout. As one of the best lyricists of the south with a silk smooth flow, Bun can almost never do wrong. The slew of guest apperances also help a lot. First of all, I really don't like Young Jeezy, and find him really annoying most of the time, but I guess if you get used to him he can be ok. He has 2 apperances on here ('Get Throwed' & 'Pushin'), which are actually 2 of the best songs on the CD, although he doesn't contribute much (the AYYEE'S and YEEAAAHHH'S on the chorus of 'Get Throwed' can get annoying). Pimp C only makes 1 apperance here (for obvious reasons), also on 'Get Throwed', and its a worthwhile one. Ludacris & T.I. make apperances here, on 'Trill Recognize Trill' & 'I'm A G' respectively, and they add some extra dopeness to both tracks. I enjoy the Ying Yang Twins from time to time, but their guest apperance on the mediocre 'Git It' just makes the song worse, not to mention the song is Bun's wackest moment of the album.While the overall product is great, songs like 'I'm Ballin', 'Hold You Down' & 'Git It' keep 'Trill' from being any more than that.Top 5 Songs (In Order):1. The Story - The story of UGK (Bun B & Pimp C), from how they met, to their record label problems, to 'Big Pimpin', to Pimp C's incarceration, its all here. Great production, and just a very interesting track to listen to.2. The Inauguration - Although its basically an inro, and only 1:51, this is easily one of the best tracks on the album. The sample sounds corny at first, but Bun's flow and the beat blend in with it perfectly and it ends up as a dope, partly politically charged track, with some of the best lines on the CD.3. I'm A G (Featuring T.I.) - Very hype track with T.I. providing a nice final verse.4. Draped Up/Draped Up H-Town Remix (Featuring Lil' Keke, Slim Thug, Chamillionaire, Paul Wall, Mike Jones, Aztek, Lil' Flip & Z-Ro) - Basically the same song (they even made a video for each), but the remix features some of the best rappers out of Houston (Scarface is in the video, but I wouldve hoped he had a verse here)5. Trill Recognize Trill (Featuring Ludacris) - Great crunk production courtesy of Lil Jon, with Ludacris pushing this track over the top.Worst Track:Git It (Featuring Ying Yang Twins) - I explained above how this is Bun's weakest performance on her, and that the Ying Yang Twins don't help much. The beat is basically a much worse version of 'Wait', and the hook just doesn't work for me.Lyrics/Substance/Subject Matter - 8/10Flow/Delivery - 9/10Production - 9/10Overall Feel - 7/10Guest Apperances - Pimp C, Z-Ro, Young Jeezy, Jay-Z, Lil' Keke, Mannie Fresh, Ludacris, Scarface, Jazze Pha, Trey Songz, Mike Jones, Baby (Birdman), T.I., Ying Yang Twins, Too Short, Juvenile, Mddl Fngz, Slim Thug, Chamillionaire, Paul Wall, Lil Flip, Aztek - 9/10 - Guests play a vital role in the success of this album, and they all deliver.Overall Rating - 8/10 - I would definately pick this up if you're interested in southern rap at all. This is some of the best material southern rap has to offer, so don't sleep.
summary: The Underground King Reclaims His Throne

reviewText: It's difficult really to fault Blur, although it would still be correct to state that they really have grown consistently better over the years.  Indeed, this certainly shows on the album, that opens with the UK Number 1 'Beetlebum'.  There are also a great deal of their earlier singles missing, although the bonus live CD more than makes up for any missing songs.At the end of the day this is a collection that really stands out, definitely alongside Oasis, who they are much compared to.  There's a good mix of indie influences and cheeky pop with great hooks.  It would be difficult to pick out a favourite although it probably depends on whether you like Blur's pop or indie leanings.  In short though, it's an album of highlights with the large variety of music sitting well alongside each other.  Most importantly though, at 28 tracks, it's a real bargain and well worth getting.

reviewText: I am really unsure of how EMI obtained the rights to Donovan's four albums SUNSHINE SUPERMAN, MELLOW YELLOW, HURDY GURDY MAN, and BARABAJAGAL, since his catalog at this time was secured by Epic Records (CBS and now a division of Sony) in the USA and were limited (by legal actions) to Pye Records in the UK.  In any event, his first two "folk" albums from Pye have been captured to varying degrees by the small independent Castle Records on CD since 2003, EMI has reissued the above four mentioned albums in 2005 and 2011, and A GIFT FROM A FLOWER TO A GARDEN was released by Collectors' Choice Music (Sony) in 2000 and is (thankfully) still in print.  Even EMI, in their liner notes to the four reissues make note of A GIFT FROM A FLOWER TO A GARDEN not being improved upon and alluding to its inclusion in the canon of Donovan's five great works.  Now with that shaky historical fact-check out of the way, let's move on to the music!This was actually my first Donovan record in my youth and it was indeed a gift.  I loved it so much I bought HURDY GURDY MAN when it came out (which became my favorite album of his).  I actually bought SUNSHINE SUPERMAN and MELLOW YELLOW after BARABAJAGAL and DONOVAN'S GREATEST HITS came out in '69, I was a late bloomer you see.  The original release of A GIFT FROM A FLOWER TO A GARDEN was a beautiful box, it was actually the first "box set" for a pop recording and was only the third ever double album set, with a 6 color (the main standard at the time was four-color) photographic print pasted to the front.  It was Donovan in his typical caftan garb holding flowers and peacock feather using an infrared light technique.  The back box photo was of Donovan visiting with the Maharishi.  Donovan was essentially the first celebrity to begin learning Transcendental Meditation under the tutelage of the Maharishi and he would influence The Beatles, Mia and Prudence Farrow, and Mike Love of The Beach Boys to take an interest.  Inside the box was a beautiful folder of art and lyrics sheets for one of the two vinyl discs "For Little Ones".  The inside top and bottom of the box contained liner notes by Donovan and lyrics to the other disc "Wear Your Love Like Heaven".  Despite the psychedelic feel of the Wear Your Love Like Heaven album, full of jaunty pop infused with lounge jazz and a splash of Celtic folk, in Donovan's notes he describes the design of the music for both albums as being divided between one for the current generation ("an age group which is gently entering marriage") and the second for the next generation ("For Little Ones", "the children of the dawning generation"), and then he loudly advocated "very youth to stop the use of all drugs and heed the quest to seek the sun".  Being one of the first initiates of the Maharishi, this no doubt came from that confluence, that Donovan had been very experimental with hallucinogens as a medium of exploration and yet he had also seen many friends move on to harder drugs, and now TM offered a "natural" means of expanding the mind.The title track to the "adult" album, Wear Your Love Like Heaven, falls into the broad spectrum of Donovan's psychedelic hippy music, lyrically ethereal with many references to dye colors; Alizarin Crimson, Rose Carmethene, Prussian Blue, Havana Lake, etc.  A hit single, the song is one of the more accessible tunes on the record along with my favorite, Sun, an acoustic vocal melody with lyrical overdubs and pretty arrangement.  Most of the other songs on the Wear Your Love Like Heaven set are lightly experimental.  Under The Greenwood Tree actually uses verse from William Shakespeare and ends with a line from The Lobster Quadrille in Alice's Adventures In Wonderland.  The Land Of Doesn't Have To Be is also a nice experiment, although I have come to love the song of the same name, arranged completely differently and with lyrics not resembling this version at all, which is found as a bonus track on MELLOW YELLOW.  For the most part, the first album has always fallen way short for me but for three or four songs.  The magic really happens with the "For Little Ones" set (which begins with track 11 on this CD).  Every song is beautifully written, performed, and arranged.  Drawing heavily from Celtic folk, before the advent of pop groups and artists doing much the same, For Little Ones has become a favorite of most adult fans of Donovan.  Yes it was intended for the children of the hippy generation, but it was readily gobbled up before they had a chance!  The songs are nuanced, they are expressive storytelling by a Bard of our generation, and they hold their beauty and attraction to this day.  They can be listened to from start to finish without ever a one of them falling short, each song as enchanting as the one before.  Like a true song-cycle, For Little Ones delivers a message in the medium and of course, coming from Donovan, the message is love.  Donovan obviously wrote the lyrics and had them printed before actual recording as you will find some disparities between listening and reading but other than Lay Of The Last Tinker, none of the changes are distracting.  Lay Of The Last Tinker is one of the most curious songs on For Little Ones, alluding to some rather adult mysteries.  In medieval times, a Tinker was a pot mender and the contents of this pot seems to be a siren or a witch!  The Enchanted Gypsy and Voyage Into The Golden Screen are my two favorites on the set, done up in a style I have been waiting for years to hear covered by the new voice of Celtic sonnets, Loreena McKinnett.  Oh well.Despite the fact that I have underhandedly given low marks to one half of the whole product, I cannot in good conscience give anything other than 5 full stars to this CD.  The remastering is perfect in clarity, volume, and acoustic translation.  Simply beautiful work by Sony.  I do love A GIFT FROM A FLOWER TO A GARDEN on the whole, as much as SUNSHINE SUPERMAN and MELLOW YELLOW (they also hold a few imperfections) and although all three albums fall short of HURDY GURDY MAN for me, taking an objective listener view, I have to admit that many others may not feel so much the same for some of the songs I might call weak.  Mind you nothing at all about this album is "bad", not by a long stretch, it is just that the majority of Wear Your Love Like Heaven (identified on this CD as "Phonograph Record 1") never has held my attention as well as For Little Ones ("Phonograph Record 2").  Some fans feel that this box set was a step down from MELLOW YELLOW and SUNSHINE SUPERMAN, other believe contrary.  Bottom line up front: it depends on your taste in music.  If you are a real fan of Donovan, there are five treasures to love from SUNSHINE through BARABAJAGAL.  If you are a casual fan, you might lean in one direction or the other, but the two releases before and after this release (found on EMI releases) are subtly different from each other.  SUNSHINE and YELLOW are flower-power psychedelic folk-pop-rock, HURDY and BARABAJAGAL are more pop-jazz-rock oriented on the whole (with frequent splashes of psychedelia and celtic).  Also on both sides of this middle, the recording quality jumped astronomically from 1967 on, and so saying, the latter two after this one were enhanced with better overall sound.  I find myself in the minority of reviewers who think this is Donovan's last great album, as I believe there was one more log to throw on the fire and perhaps even one more after that!I do know one thing:  this album was indeed a gift from a flower to a garden!
