reviewText: Steve Albini may be a genius but that doesn't make this album enjoyable.  Albini really is a great producer (sorry..."studio engineer") and the level of innovation he brings to his guitar playing puts Thurston Moore to shame.  When it comes to unique guitar tones and sounds, the only guy in Albini's league is the great Kevin Shields of My Bloody Valentine.  But Albini's virtuosity is actually Shellac's biggest downfall.  Albini has said several times in interviews that he doesn't care about songwriting, just sound.  This obsession with sound and total disregard for songs renders "At Action Park" nothing more than a nice art project no matter how physically powerful and inventive the playing is.  "My Black Ass,"  "Song For The Minerals" and "The Admiral" all sound great, but they are all essentially the same.  Albini starts out with a crazy-sounding but ultimately repetitive guitar figure and then the rhythm section comes in with awkward time signatures to try to mask the inherent hollowness of each song.  Also, most of Albini's vocals are incomprehensible here so we don't get the wicked sense of humor that elevated his (superior but still overrated) old band Big Black.  At Action Park is great to listen to if you're interested in studio recording techniques and is even enjoyable in small doses when you're in the mood for some brutal pounding and nothing more, but on repeated listens it just doesn't hold up.  Albini should stick to recording other artists who actually know how to write songs because his studio techniques really are incredible and he's done amazing work behind the boards for PJ harvey, Jesus Lizard, Dirty Three, Mclusky, and though he hates to admit it, The Pixies.  I'd reccomend buying any Albini-recorded albums by the above listed artists instead of blowing your money on Shellac's three (interchangable) albums.

reviewText: I have been a fan of R. Kelly for a long time and when I heard that TP-2 was coming out, I could not wait, especially after hearing the remarkable "I Wish" and "To the Homies That We Lost". At first it seemed like this was going to be a great album with the interesting arrangement of "Strip For You", but I was dissapointed by the next five tracks since they were quite mediocre and overly repetitious. Many critics have said the R. Kelly is a little repetitive, but I never really agreed until hearing these songs. "Fiesta was nice", the guitar a little remeniscent of "Did You Ever Think" for "R". "The Real R. Kelly" was funny at first but not enough to save the somewhat boring "One Me". At last we came to a nice stretch "I Wish", "I Decided", "To The Homies That We Lost", "All I Really Want", "Feelin' On Yo Booty" and "The Storm Is Over". Sadly these tracks are still not enough to save this album. Even the photography of a more thuggish-looking R. Kelly were no way as good as the classy material used in the "R" liner notes. On another note, I read recently a review by someone saying that R Kelly's on a downward spiral into thuggery. I feel that R always had that thug persona bubbling at the surface and I feel that it should not interfere with his music, but if I discovered that it is the cause of this mediocre album, I would be most disappointed.Honestly, I would recommend that you do NOT buy this album and instead invest in "R". It has a much better mix and of a higher class. "R" is still one of my favourite albums after many years of listening. If you really like the singles such as I Wish and Feelin' On Yo Booty (really good remix) purchase them instead and ignore this album. That may give R the message that he should rethink his strategy.

reviewerName: Wayne Klein "If at first the idea is not absu...
reviewText: Chrissie Hynde channels her angst on their latest...oh wait a second this is by the Yeah Yeah Yeah's! This album might have been something in 1979 but it's a bit derivative and the musical trio doesn't offer much depth here. Perhaps by their next album they'll begin to discover their sound. In the meantime, they may want to tune their instruments a bit.To be fair, everyone has to start somewhere. The Yeahx3 aren't bad. They fit well into the same uncomfortably narrow niche as many other garage bands. That definition isn't quite fair, though, as it seems the bulk of the bands that have been lumped together into this genre have little to nothing in common. I'd say the same is true here for the Yeahx3. While their music isn't all that original or earthshattering, there is potential here.Perhaps the worst part for this band is the fact that everyone will define them by the conventions of the "garage" genre. It fits them (like everyone else lumped together in this category) like a poorly tailored suit.Music fans that missed The Pretenders, The Clash or any other band that stuck middle finger in the air in defiance, will probably appreciate The Yeah Yeah Yeah's. The buzz that surrounds this is deserved although somewhat premature. Hype has snuffed out the life of many bands before they had the chance to flourish and the same could happen here as well. Hopefully the members of this band will stick to their guns and try to develop their own individual sound.Although the album isn't all that adventurous (it sticks to very basic melodies and, like the Ramones, keeps the songs to a minimum running time), these folks might just have some merit somewhere down the line.  Given time they could potentially make a great album or flame out like dozens of other promising bands. Unfortunately, only time will tell and this album is a bit underwhelming.

reviewerName: M. A. Scott "Rock and Classical music fan"
reviewText: This may be heresy to some people, but Disraeli Gears is tied with "Days of future past" by the Moody blues as the best rock album of 1967. Yes, I even think both of them are better than Sgt.Peppers by the Beatles! The other albums just about as good as this from the late 60's are the Moody Blues "On the threshold of a dream", "Led Zeppelin II", and "Abbey Road" by the Beatles. This is not nearly as bluesy as "Fresh Cream", but it's got more good songs than that one does. I won't mention the two main hits because everybody knows those epic tracks, but the tunes that I like best are "SWLABR", "Tales Of Brave Ulysses", "Dance the night away", "World of pain", "Take it back", and "Blue Condition". I don't have this remastered version, but have the first issue from the 80's, and it sounds just right to me sonically. This is the only Cream album that I ever liked totally, but each album had at least a handful of good tunes. Enjoy!!!

reviewText: I am not, wasn't anyway, a follower of Coheed and Cambria.  I bought "Burning Star" based upon an AMG review which referenced Queensryche.  I'm a huge QR fan, so figured I'd check out Coheed and Cambria.  I was blown away by this album.It's difficult to categorize the band, definitely prog-metal, but unlike any other I've heard before.  There are certainly similarities to QR and Dream Theater, but neither band is able to come up with the consistent hooks that Coheed and Cambria have throughout "Burning Star."  Claudio Sanchez's vocal style is very much Geddy Lee, and there are other similarities to Rush, but they are very different bands.  Coheed and Cambria's tunes are very layered, powerful vocals, driving guitars and percussion, and some really imaginative backing vocals.  "Burning Star" is fantastic throughout, some of the most powerful and hook laden prog-metal I've heard in a long time, maybe ever.

reviewText: Those Brits will fall for ANYTHING. Frankie madness swept England in the mid Eighties and was literally over before it began. One dud album later ( the lamentable Liverpool ) and it was all over except for the sobbing. As for "Pleasuredome", pure marketing genius is the strongest force behind it. People were so hyped by the singles Relax and Two Tribes, all those catchy slogans on the tee shirts and the media frenzy, that by the time this bloated beast arrived, it was snapped up by the truckload, apparently with no regard to its contents. If Pleasuredome were pared down to a single album, it would be simply perfect. A double album, however, was not only unnecessary, but criminal, and a complete joke on the frenzied public. The three singles ( the third being the gorgeous ballad the Power of Love ) plus the epic title track and a few of the more understated songs like Black Night White Light and the Ballad of 32 would make it one terrific album. But the covers ( among them War, Born to Run, and San Jose ) are laughable in both their selection and excecution, and spoil what otherwise could have been a pristine and possibly classic album. The same goes for throwaways like Krisco Kisses and Only Star in Heaven. By all means, if you love the eighties ( and lets face it, who doesn't ) get this album. The playing is tight, the production is superb ( take ANOTHER bow, Trevor Horn ) and there are a handful of great songs. But  be warned : keep your finger close to the "skip" button on your cd player, you'll need it.

reviewText: I'm a sucker for some good indie pop and Bastille fills that void admirably. This is an album of tunes impeccably produced, constructed, and executed to maximum effect.By now hits like "Flaws", "Pompeii", and "Things We Lost in the Fire" have probably graced your ears. If you dig those songs then this record will most likely please you, as most of the tracks here follow in a similar vain. Songs like "Daniel in the Den", "These Streets", and "Icarus" are filled to the brim with emotion and effervescent melodies that make you want to interact with the songs and keep listening. In fact, I'd rank "Laura Palmer" as one of the best songs of 2013, a soaring and ambitious track that delivers everything I love in a song: grand instrumentation, big emotion, and superb production. I can't get enough of it.The only thing that holds this album back is the lack of diversity present in many of these songs. As good as the group is they also have a tendency to stick with a similar sound that makes a few of the tracks bleed together. This gives the album cohesion and for that they should be commended, yet it would have been nice to see them branch out and try something a bit different on some of these tunes. Here's hoping that they continue to expand and deliver another great album in the near future.

reviewText: Rob Thomas' "Cradlesong" is another great set.  His tunes sound different from much of the other music.  On this set, "Someday" is one of my favorites while it feels slow but sounds full with the sentimental chorus, "Maybe someday we'll figure all this out; We'll put an end to all our doubt, try to find a way to just feel better now."  "Mockingbird" also catches my ear with its driving lead guitar, throbbing rhythm guitar & Rob's melody hitting the higher register, "Everybody else is smiling."  "Wonderful" also has a great hook-filled chorus that seduces you with its catchy tune as Thomas challenges with a grueling self-assessment, "Guess I'm past my prime & now I'm over-rated, over dressed & overstated."  Thomas dives deep while keeping the whole thing entertaining.  His is a fascinating artistry.  Enjoy!

reviewText: Luis Mejia (son) - After the very well critisized Madman Across The Water and the stunningly produced Honky Chateau, Elton John goes through a pop basis and more difficult songs, leaving the stage of simple piano ballads.This album is an excellent work by Elton, debut at 1973, the album marked a brilliant fame in USA, having some of his most catchy, simple, mellodic, classic and creative moods of all of Elton's albums. Not his best work,  yet a fantastic album wich stablish his era of piano rock and catchy sounds with a simple and familiar style. Don't Shoot Me I'm Only The Piano Player keeps a fresh and juvenile mood in every song, having graceful and imaginative compositions, also very humorous, still without loosing all of his piano ballad basis. The production is also fantastic but not as great as Honky Chateau.This album keeps a structure that make every song fit perfectly with the other, making the whole album worth and all alike, like the simple, pop and mellodic tracks Daniel, which is the 2nd most famous track, and Blues For Baby And Me, the dramatic, thematic, suburban songs like Midnight Creeper and Have Mercy On The Criminal, the catchy, beautiful and joyful songs High Flying Bird, Elderberry Wine and Crocodile Rck (one of my personal favorites and the most famous song in this album), the humorous, refreshing tracks like I'm Gonna Be A Teenage Idol and Teacher I Need You, and the exagerated but consistent composition Texan Love Song.As I said before, Elton's aspirations changed a lot in this album, applying a consistent mixture of popular music with a joyful rock and roll. His piano performance is seen much better in past albums, where he kept piano as the basis of his compositions, but its enjoyable as well. Bernie Taupin lyrics are much more creative and juvenile, leaving deep and melancholic lyrics and entering in this mood, which is certainly one of the aspects that make the 70's Elton's best era. The band performs with dedication and great rythm, leaving the album just as what it is, a bright and stylish album.In conclussion this album keeps a lot of originality and the start of piano rock and familiar, popular sounds, very comprehensible, fresh and juvenile.
summary: I remember when rock was young...

reviewText: After the promising debut album "September 000" and the brilliant break-out album "Now Here Is Nowhere" in 2004, the Screat Machines come back with their third album."Ten Silver Drops" (8 tracks, 45 min.) is a mixed affair. The album starts off very tentatively with "Alone, Jealous and Stoned", a lazy track whallowing in self-pity (the album reflects the hard times several of the guys in the band went through in their personal lives). It is really a head-scratcher that this is the opening track. Things get better with "Lightning Blue Eyes", a great uptempo track, setting the stage for the monster track of the album, the 8+ min. epic "Daddy's In the Doldrums", evoking the bombastic sound found on "Now Here Is Nowhere". It is followed by the best track on the album, "I Hate Pretending", with a great moog-synthesizer sound reminiscent of ELP's "Lucky Man". The remaining three tracks are quite forgettable, unfortunately, and they go on too long (that, with the album has only 8 tracks).I am a huge fan of the band, and can't help but feel disappointed by this album. Yes, there are great momnets, but there are too many unfocused, down-beat tracks that go "nowhere", so in all this is a step back from "Now Here Is Nowhere", one of the best albums of 2004. That said, the Secret Machines are one of the best live acts out there today, and if you have a chance to see them in concert, don't miss it, you won't be disappointed!

It is followed by the best track on the album, "I Hate Pretending", with a great moog-synthesizer sound reminiscent of ELP's "Lucky Man". they go on too long (that, with the album has only 8 tracks).I am a huge fan of the band, and can't help but feel disappointed by this album. Yes, there are great momnets, but there are too many unfocused, down-beat tracks that go "nowhere", so in all this is a step back from "Now Here Is Nowhere", one of the best albums of 2004. That said, the Secret Machines are one of the best live acts out there today, and if you have a chance to see them in concert, don't miss it, you won't be disappointed!

reviewText: "The Future" from 1992 was Cohen's follow -up to his big comeback album "I'm Your Man" from 1988. "The Future" appears a natural extension of its predecessor, where Cohen had turned towars a "modern" 1980's sound with arrangements marked by both big sound and drama.The album is Cohen's longest  studioalbum , and couple of the less interesting track could easily have been omitted. His covers of "Be for Real" and Irving Berlin's "Always" are not particularly interesting , and the closing instrumental number "Tacoma Trailer" doesn't really add much to the album.The rest of the album is, in turn, first-class material and the majority of these songs soon became live favorites . The songs "The Future", " Waiting for the Miracle", " Closing Time", "Anthem" and "Democracy" are still often found Cohen's live repertoire-lists.These are also the five songs that make the album great . "The Future" is for Cohen an unusual up-beat number spiced with doomsday lyrics. "Waiting for the Miracle" is beautiful song written in collaboration with Sharon Robinson, who would later to play an even greater role in Cohen's musical development. A fine tune and excitingly arranged with funny little fragments of melody; for example, the funny whistle thing."Closing Time" won the Juno Award for Best Music Video in 1993. The song has a great chorus and is very catchy, not least because the great female voices that back up so perfectly . "Anthem" is a magnificent song with a whole choir them to back up on the chorus, and it is the song with the suggestive line "There is a crack in everything , that's how the light gets in". "Democracy" is a song that in a way continues the tone of "I'm Your Man"'s "First We Take Manhanttan", the lyrics are extensive long open to many different interpretations, I'm sure.The songs on the album are relatively long; most from five to eight minutes, which explains the long playing-time - most of them bear their lenghts fine. There are female voices on most tracks, which has become a kind of hallmark for Cohen and as a whole is "The Future" one of his very best albums .

reviewText: Many of us are very familiar with ABBA's songs because we have heard them often over the years. Personally, I knew of them from a distance and never researched them until recently. Living in Germany placed me in the thick of the ABBA Fan Club as they are revered here in Europe. There are enough ABBA fans here to pack any venue where they would perform, believe that. Already familiar with tracks such as "Dancing Queen", "Take A Chance On Me" and "Mamma Mia", I can now associate ever so closely with their string of hits. More importantly, this music is nostalgic and full of great, feel good vibes. For that reason alone ABBA Gold is worth having in your collection. Maybe you already do or maybe, like me, you already loved them and didn't even know it.EnjoyDJ Come of Age

reviewText: Perfect From Now On is Built to Spill's third album and gained widespread attention when it was released in 1997. A long vast & epic voyage through 8 noise shifting songs. Perfect From Now On was at the time their tightest sounding album yet, and first major-label release on Warner Bros. Perfect from Now On is filled w/ wailing guitar effects and groove-laden blissful jams. So many twists and turns throughout. Just more of a broadened scope, deeper range and timelessness here.Yes, these are LONG songs, approaching times between 5 and 9 minutes each. This release reminds me a bit of Neutral Milk Hotel. PERFECT FROM NOW ON is filled with colorful rawness, a beautiful mess.While their next album "Keep It Like A Secret" is catchier, shorter and poppy.At this time(1997) the band consists of Doug Martsch: singer/guitarist - his vocals are farther ranging, more matured & more exquisite then on "There's Nothing Wrong With Love," Along w/ band -also adding MORE muscle, depth & volume; takes it's listener on a real experience of adventureBrett Netson: bass & guitar; and drummer Scott Plouf.Built to Spill is one of the more important talented bands that more people need to hear. Constantly changing styles and band members w/ each release. And this is their most creative, mesmerizing, most psychadelic sound put out by them. Favorite song: "Kicked It In the Sun." - I also LOVE opener: "Randy Described Eternity" - "I Would Hurt A Fly" - "Velvet Waltz" - "Untrustable/Part 2."To me this is close to PERFECTION and my Favorite Built to Spill record so far as of 2007. 5 stars!

reviewText: The title refers to one of the most beautiful, unique songs I have heard in my life. Tender, sad, wistful, and at times angry. These all apply to the feelings Tori Amos expresses throughout Scarlet's Walk, which is a masterpiece in every sense of the word - beautiful, timeless, socially relevant, melodic, and poetic.I wasn't always a Tori Amos fan. If you would have asked me a month ago, I probably wouldn't have known anything about her. I stumbled across this album by accident - the cover artwork and the names of songs captured my imagination. The picture of Tori standing alone in the road is really stunning and conveys the mood of this album - a road trip after the tragic events of September eleventh. It is a fictional epic story of love, heartbreak, and the lives of people encountered during a troubled time...from aging porn stars (Amber Waves), gay people who die unnoticed in our "caring" yet careless world (Taxi Ride), and a love that passes us by but the memories remain to open like a favorite book (A Sorta Fairtytale). Tori Amos gives us a very sensitive and cathartic look at the individual people that make up America. Inside you will find a map of all the places she visited and wrote particular songs.I used to think Tori Amos was rather strange and different...but I only thought so because I had never actually heard any of her music. It is rarely if ever played on the rado, it seems. I'm just lucky that I was able to experience Tori's music, because it has become a very important part of my life. The lyrics to Your Cloud are all my feelings put into a song. Thank you, Tori.

reviewText: I owned Joan Jett's album "Up Your Alley" on cassette tape along with Pat Benatar's "Wide Awake In Dreamland", which were both issued by Epic Records the same year (1988; back then, Pat's label, Chrysalis, was owned by Epic).  These two albums were the best of that year.  The hit tune "I Hate Myself For Loving You" is now overdone to death as the NBC Sunday Night Football jingle, but I loved Joan's intimate guitar on "Little Liar", her best track on the album.Overall, this album ranks up there with "Bad Reputation" and "I Love Rock & Roll" as one of Joan's three hallmarks of her recording career.  Too bad she and Pat Benatar couldn't have done at least one duet--their combined vocals and guitars would have sounded great together.

reviewText: As an example of musical philosophy, this album seems closest to the themes of the eternal return.  The title song, "Coming Around Again," is credited as being from the Paramount Motion Picture "Heartburn."  The song "As Time Goes By," written by Herman Hupfeld in 1931, is famous from the movie "Casablanca" if not from Woody Allen's obsession with that movie in "Play It Again, Sam."  The song "Itsy Bitsy Spider" based on the Original Nursery Rhyme at the end of the CD brings in the "Coming Around Again" theme as a counter-melody.  The production is tremendous.Actually, what I like most about this CD is the song "Do the Walls Come Down."  It might be all one question, as the written text (Words by Carly Simon) in the CD liner notes only has one question mark, at the end of the last line:  "Like a stowaway?"  There is a peircing instrumental solo in that song which seems to be burned into my mind, credited in the notes to Michael Brecker on a Steiner Electronic Wind Instrument.  It reminds me of Bob Dylan singing about penny-whistles in the song "Desolation Row."  As Freud might have noticed, "Nothing like a vivid dream to take you back again."  I like to play this CD to feel life at the maximum impact level.

reviewText: An early collection of studio recordings from 1950 and 1949, The appropriately titled "Birth Of Cool" isone of Jazz's first classic long player records.  Recorded for Capitol Records, Miles Davis leads a group ofvirtuosic instrumentalists through a incredible set of free form jazz compositions.  As the title suggests, this recordmarked the birth of a new kind of jazz.  The eleven songs presented here use more of a "big band" arrangement than mostother types of jazz, and they are generally short; most clock in at around three minutes. So unlike most free form jazzwhich tends to meander all over the place, most of the solos and breaks here stay in place and, therefore, add a sense ofcohesiveness to the record.  Yet regardless of how short and cohesive the songs are, this is certainly not pop music, asmost of the songs don't follow conventional pop song structure.This genre of jazz is known as West Coast Jazz or simply "cool".  And it's easy to see why it's called cool becauseregardless of how chaotic or intense the music gets, there is a sense of restraint and mood.  The music is never too hot,so one can cool off to it if you get my point. This was indeed the birth of a new era of jazz and jazz has never soundedquite the same since.This is a great introduction to Miles Davis' body of work not to mention an essential listen for serious jazz fans.  Thosewho are more used to his more experiemental work like "Kind Of Blue" and "Bitches Brew" might have a harder time gettinginto this record, but the effort is worth it.

reviewText: For some reason this was (ironically) the last of the classic 7 Moody Blues album's to really grow on me.I don't know what it was on first listen that just kind of made me toss it off as their weakest effort.Only recently did I give it another chance.What a Killer album!Perhaps because the recording was diffirent than any other before it. Maybe because I just stereotyped it as the final album that the band had to release to fulfill a recording contract type of deal.I don't know,but even though my opinion may change in a month or two right now this is my favorite,maybe second favorite Moodie's album ever.I'll be the first to tell you that I've thought that at one time or another about each and every one of their albums(at least the first seven).But the magic on this album has a matured fulfilled feeling about it that is really quite impressive.The vocals and instrumentation are very strong on each and every song.My personal favorite's are "New Horizons","For my Lady", and "Isn't life Strange" which are of course back to back on the album which makes it almost impossible for me to listen to one of these song's without the other two."I'm just a singer" is a perfect way to not only end the album,but to also end the so called classic era of The Moody Blues career.It's only fitting that this would be last of their first seven albums to click with me and to anyone else my age(born in 86)I would recommend getting into their album's in order of their creation starting of course with "Day's of Future Passed".There is definitely something special and unique about the "Seventh Sojourn" of the Moody Blues.

reviewText: This review is for the three albums which make up the SCHMILSSON era of Harry Nilsson's music, that which some regard as his best recording period, despite the fact that the central album in the trilogy has consistently received some of his lowest marks and remarks.  However you look at it, SCHMILSSON albums are the product of a new, a second era, in Nilsson's catalogue, and most remarkably, perhaps his most experimental and dynamic vocals ever delivered.  Harry Nilsson had matured over the course of 4 albums, from 1967 to 1970, and in 1971 he released what would be his last album of "whimsical sweetness", and then took his first two albums to the engineering board for a revamp and re-recorded many vocals for them to release one of the, if not the, first ever remix album in modern recording history.  Then, to quote the radiommercials of the day "Harry's got a rock album!"  ...and so it began.NILSSON SCHMILSSONIt has been on just about every Top This or Top That list for 40 years as of last month.  It was nominated for the Grammy for Album of the Year 1971 (just edged out by the historic Bridge Over Troubled Water, oh well, I can't complain too much), won the Grammy for Best Male Vocal Performance for the song Without You (when Mariah Carey was only a year old!), a song which stayed on two Billboard charts number one positions for five weeks, was a number one single in every English-speaking country on the planet, the album rode the top 3 for weeks, and spawned two more hit singles, and went gold inside of 4 months.  Produced by the legendary Richard Perry and featuring a musical cast of who's who talent from the era, including Elton John's early band and Eric Clapton's drummer, NILSSON SCHMILSSON is the paean of classic rock era albums.  Schmilsson should be included in every audiophile's top 10 list whether for best recorded album, best engineered album, best vocal performance, the lists go on!  Schmilsson is an all around feel good monster of rock, pop, R&B;, adult contemporary, and raw rock and soul.  It is a Beatlemaniac's dream come true, a Beatles album after the breakup without the Beatles, a fun frolic through the music that defined the early 70's when almost everything being produced was "progressive". NILSSON SINGS NEWMAN very nearly killed his career following a budding success with the previous HARRY album.  One can speculate that the critical success outweighed the sales figures in terms of "successful" since the album of nothing but Randy Newman covers was hailed by several reviewers as a pinnacle of achievement, but if you know Harry's history, he held his head high and forged on with his own plans and blessed by good management at RCA who knew a good thing when they saw and heard it, Harry never wavered.  Ironically, '71 became his banner year.  The year that ended with the mega-monster SCHMILSSON, also ironic because it was actually perfectly mainstream for the progressive rock development of the year.  Harry moved into composition of songs that could only be heard as direct descendants and evolved from the continuous growth of the Beatles music up to 1970.  It was as if he embodied their souls for another year and advanced their techniques and sounds into his own musical achievement.  His covers on the album were also tantamount to historic recordings!  He took a rather beatlesque song by Beatlesque Apple recording group Badfinger, a guitar strummed medium speed ballad, "Without You", rearranged it for emotive piano lead, and sang it three octaves into music history as one of the most beautiful, heart-breaking love songs, to ever hit the radio waves.  The recording now stands as nearly untouchable and those who try either hit or seriously miss.  Mariah got lucky with it.  In any event, the release of the single sent crowds after the LP and everyone was richly rewarded with ample happiness.  In addition to "Without You", Harry covered a 1947 blues song, "Early In The Morning" which became a Ray Charles standard in 1961 and he covers it mostly a la Ray Charles with some incredible vocal range exercising.  The other cover is the early rock'n roll hit by Shirley & Lee (1956), "Let The Good Times Roll", a fairly faithful rendition with Nilsson again exercising his chops and playfully getting carried away.  These covers were gravy however on an already impeccably written and produced collection of magic!  Yes..."Without You" is certainly the centerpiece of the whole album, but it is far from being the only standout.  One has to envision that Harry and his new (at the time) producer Richard Perry worked some incantations to get the song order, the emotional feeling rollercoaster, the engineering, every single dust particle in perfection!  It is almost as if the album could have been anything and failed, but what they did with it ended up as perfection in art.  There are very few albums I can easily compare to SCHMILSSON with the same conviction of emotional endorsement. For pure power and soul, if it's your thing, you will gravitate to this track again and again. Surprisingly fresh when it was first introduced, the song has not lost any of its charm and remains a favorite in rotation of many FM radio stations aimed at retro audiences. The original recording, beautifully sung with piano sans orchestra is hidden at the end of the remasted CD of The Point!  (see below).  If you are bound and determined to own only one Harry Nilsson recording this is the one to profit from.  BMG has remastered the sound wonderfully and tacked on 7 bonus tracks: (1) a Spanish language single release of "Without You" which became a #1 hit in Latin America, (2) "How Can I Be Sure", a flippant introspective tongue in cheek serio-comedic diddy that would have fit on the follow-up Son OF Schmilsson, (3) a nicely recorded demo of The Moonbeam Song arranged with different lead instruments, (4) "Lamaze" is just plain hilarious, not quite a song but more a comedy routine on piano, it cannot be described without spoilers so just listen and laugh, (5) "Old Forgotten Soldier" is another piece that would have fit perfectly in with Son Of... musically but slightly more on the serious side, (6) a "demo" version, more of an alternate take of "Gotta Get Up", not yet fully formed with more a sailors shanty to it, and finally (7) a series of radio spots for the original album release, worth one listen and then disposable after that.  You could live without these bonuses but five out of the seven are essential material to Nilsson fans even casual fans are likely to move them onto the mp3 player so with the remastered sound and these extra small treats, Sony BMG can only get my sincerest thanks, no matter how I truly feel about the parent company.SON OF SCHMILSSONIf you remember the line form Pink Floyd's song Have A Cigar, where it's sung "We're so happy we can hardly count!", that is what the record producers and accountants at RCA were doing after the release of NILSSON SCHMILSSON and immediately the pressure was on for a follow-up and they want more of the same!  Well, if you have read this far, and if you have my reviews for his previous albums, you are pretty well acquainted with the man and his eccentricities.  No, Harry did not bounce into the studio and whip out another monster hit full of audience-friendly singles and complex progressive rock.  No...no he didn't do that.  SON OF SCHMILSSON was a case where the apple did fall far from the tree.  Unlike its father, Son Of was a tale of eccentric bawdiness, crass humor, juvenile humor, and some may have even thought it a blunt stick.  True Nilsson fans loved the hell out it, while fans of SCHMILSSON alone were soon to divorce themselves from the album, ergo it could be found in 2nd hand record shops easily, soon after its release.  My, my, Harry, what have you done?  Even some of his long time but more conservative fans, who followed him from the outset to The Point! and on the Schmilsson just couldn't find redemption in this one.  But I ask, why?  Anyone with a brain in his head and eyes open to the nature of the beast can easily see that sometimes it is going to do what a beast does, it acts like a beast and follows its own natural bent.  And Nilsson, no matter how much we guffaw about it, had a wickedly funny side to him that we only caught glimpses of before.  So we bought our SON OF SCHMILSSON album, brought it home and plopped the platter on the turntable.  "Take 54" is sung seriously out of tune by an alter ego of Harry Nilsson who is quite upset about his devolving relationship with the girl, who seems to ignore the recording studio door "with the red light on it".  He sang his "balls off for you, baby" and how do you repay him?  Well after that the song fades into the REM sleep of a snoring Richard Perry who awakens to creepy sound effects and a Hammer Horror voice shouting "Son of Schmilsson", etc.  Imagine That!  The first track is a radio commercial!  Well we can easily dismiss that one, besides, the 2nd song, "Remember" is a lovely, Christmas-ey, Harry Nilsson song that everyone loves.  Yes it is radio friendly, has nice string arrangement and piano work, pretty vocals, a homey message, and we are on our way!  To "Joy", a country-western parody that will have you holding your belly from achingly funny if you have never heard it before, it naturally segues, lyrically and musically into "Turn On Your Radio", another nice Nilsson tune that almost hearkens back to the early Nilsson days, okay we have one clunker so far, one pretty, one funny, and one reminiscing song.  So the final song on side one of the record is coming.  It's called "You're Breaking My Heart", aw this must be a tear-jerker, get your hankies out... So loud raucous rampaging horns accompanying Harry on vocals and electric piano, acoustic piano by Nicky Hopkins, Klaus Voorman on bass and sax, Peter Frampton on lead electric guitar and George Harrison on slide guitar, this is what you hear on You're Breaking My Heart.  That...and the lyrics that accusingly alarm "You're breaking my heart, you're tearing it apart, so [expletive deleted] you!"  Yes, Harry dropped the F-bomb in song, probably the first time on record since The Fish Cheer by Country Joe at Woodstock, and year earlier than Pink Floyd used the vulgar form of male cow excrement in "Money".  My my!  How many teenagers were playing this record with the door open when Mom and Dad were within hailing distance?  The way I figure it, Harry was going through that messy divorce thing at the time and this song probably just FELT really really good at the time ("I dunno, I was really drunk at the time...").  Quick Junior!  Turn the record over before Mom comes to the door, turn it up and you can't hear her knocking!  Yeeeeeaaaahhh!  Yeah that's the refrain that makes "Spaceman" such a terrific song!  First of all, Elton beat Harry to the launching pad but Harry used better fuel and it's not burning out, he's just stuck spinning around the world and the bop vocal backing has so much more energy than that silly old "rocket man".  Listen to them both now and tell me which one sounds "dated".  They were released within three months of each other so my guess is it will boil down to who actually recorded theirs first!  `Sides, Ringo plays drums on this one!!!  Okay, concession here, Elton's version is supposed to be dramatic, Harry's song is most definitely humorous, or at least anecdotal.  "The Lottery Song" is cute little diddy about striking it rich and moving to Vegas to be famous.  It has everything a cute little diddy should have, charm, wit, and greed.  Ah!  Here comes a reprise of "Remember", "long ago...far away...[burp!]...excuse me!"  oh Harry yer jess so funny!  But dig that rocking rhythm guitar and drums, Ringo on drums and Ray Cooper on congas, Frampton and Chris Spedding on dual lead guitars, Nicky Hopkins, Klaus again, and Bobby Keys on tenor sax, all rocking out to The El Dorados doo-wop Crazy Little Mama "At My Front Door"!  and that one is followed by a slow building blues-rock "Ambush" which is very hard to decide if it is a serious anti-war thumping chant, or a tongue in cheek poke at something else, by now you are just so jaded, but it's a terrific song!  And it is a great vocal exercise by Harry.  Then Harry decided to go to a British old-folks home and whoop up a sing-a-long with the boys and girls, "I'd Rather Be Dead" ("than wet my bed").  Now THIS is humor!  (actually it grows on you with age, almost 40 years later I can say I love it more today than when I used to skip it outright).  So how does one end an album filled with redolent debauchery and obtuse jokes?  One writes and records a song dedicated to The World.  In fact, you equate the World to a Girl and write a love song for "her", start it out in a quasi-island jibe with poor Caribbean Ricky Ricardo accent (be sure to include gargle and spit during the interlude), and then slow it down to an orchestrated love ballad ("I love the way you wear your trees") ending in a deeply efficacious line, "tell her she's beautiful, roll the world over, and give her a kiss...and a feel".  Yes, yes!  It's all in good fun, and when was the last time you listened to music and had good childish laugh?  Live a little!  This is the Harry Nilsson who got bombed with John Lennon and together headed down to The Troubador to heckle The Smothers Brothers until they got thrown out!  The cover must have given you SOME indication, I mean for Pete's Sake, Dracula?  By the way, his next project was a silly-ass movie starring himself and Ringo Starr, called...wait for it...Son Of Dracula!  Okay, one of the worst bombs in movie history but great soundtrack!  Most of the songs are from Schmilsson and Son Of Schmilsson, and it boasted one minor hit single itself, "Daybreak" which has finally found its way onto this album as a bonus track for the BMG remaster release.  It sounds so much better than the poor quality recording that was used in some compilation albums.  There are other bonus tracks to boost this romper room romp and add to the comedic frolick but the bottom line is this, serious now folks, SON OF SCHMILSSON was quite definitely for The Nilsson Fan and for the same public who got a kick out of Benny Hill and Monty Python, so if that is not your bag, then by all means, don't waste your money and skip this album.  If you want "serious music" buy yourselves the next Schmilsson classic, A LITTLE TOUCH OF SCHMILSSON IN THE NIGHT, and be sure to get the fully evolved version as Nilsson intended it to be.  Son Of... is meant to be for kicks and giggles but it has some real gems on it too.  Remember, At My Front Door (the only non-Nilsson written song on the album), Ambush, and Spaceman being the more progressive ones and who cannot love the finale of "The Most Beautiful World In The World"?  LOVE IT!!!A LITTLE TOUCH OF SCHMILSSON IN THE NIGHTBeholding him, plucks comfort from his looks:A largess universal like the sunHis liberal eye doth give to every one,Thawing cold fear, that mean and gentle all,Behold, as may unworthiness define,A little touch of Harry in the night.(William Shakespeare, Henry V, Act IV, Prologue)Henry the 5th, affectionately called "Harry" by his battle-weary troops, comforted his men in the field before the morning's charge against the enemy, "A little touch of Harry in the night", and these nocturnal visits is where Harry Nilsson derived the title for an album of music; from a pop-rock artist no less, in 1973 no less, from "The Great American Songbook".  It was this concept which Harry had, to address the music of our pre-rock and roll, pre-modern era, songs of warmth and comfort, from the stalwarts of 20th century composition, and to tackle songs which require, by definition, the greatest of vocal acrobatics, and vocal beauty.  Harry's voice, and this music, were a match made in heaven.  This was, again, another step up, a very risky and very challenging task."The Great American Songbook" is a hypothetical construct that "seeks to represent the best American songs of the 20th century principally from Broadway theatre, musical theatre, and Hollywood musicals, from the 1920s to 1960, including dozens of songs of enduring popularity."  (Alec Wilder)Mainly through the work of Alec Wilder, in 1972, after over a decade of research, he published what is now considered the "canon" of American Popular Song, beginning in 1900 and ending it in 1950 with the near advent of rock and roll.  The Great American Songbook is essentially a ranking and study of composers and creative efforts.  He identifies specifically Jerome Kern, Irving Berlin, George Gershwin, Richard Rodgers, Cole Porter, Harold Arlen, Vincent Youmans, Arthur Schwartz, Burton Lane, Hugh Martin, and Vernon Duke.  Then he deemed the following "The Great Craftsmen": Hoagy Carmichael, Walter Donaldson, Harry Warren, Isham Jones, Jimmy McHugh, Duke Ellington, Fred Ahlert, Richard A. Whiting, Ray Noble, John Green, Rube Bloom, and Jimmy Van Heusen.  Lastly he concluded his research with a 67 page chapter of "Outstanding Individual Songs" which were singled out from the works of Harold Arlen, Irving Berlin, Nacio Herb Brown, Hoagy Carmichael, Walter Donaldson, Vernon Duke, Duke Ellington, Sammy Fain, George and Ira Gershwin, Ray Henderson, Herman Hupfeld, Bart Howard, Isham Jones, Jerome Kern, Frank Loesser, Jimmy McHugh, Johnny Mercer, Cole Porter, Rodgers and Hart, Rodgers and Hammerstein, Harry Ruby and Bert Kalmar, Arthur Schwartz and Howard Dietz, Jule Styne, Jimmy Van Heusen, Harry Warren, Richard Whiting, Jack Yellen, Vincent Youmans, and Victor Young.There is a style and a structure which is categorically definable to all of the song craft in the songbook, from the composers above, but that would require a musicology degree and more technical proficiency than this writer has.  I can, however, with complete confidence, identify A LITTLE TOUCH OF SCHMILSSON IN THE NIGHT as a singular supreme effort which perfectly resonates with that style and structure which makes the songs he worked from the lists above something more than total enlightenment.There has been a recent revival of The Great American Songbook in the last two decades, especially since Rod Stewart began his gravelly crooning (which answers the question, exactly just how many American Songbook albums can someone make?) to the ad infinitum point of stomach churning.  Actually, believe it or not, it began in 1970 with Ringo Starr's Sentimental Journey album, his first after the breakup of The Beatles.  It was critically praised but not a terrific seller on the market.  Harry was next in 1973 with this album.  Shortly after Nilsson's album, Bryan Ferry of Roxy Music released a similar experiment, These Foolish Things, and then in 1978 Willie Nelson released his collection Stardust which is still his most endearing album to date.  Linda Ronstadt of course released a trilogy with Nelson Riddle starting in '83 and in '91 Natalie Cole did that Unforgettable "duet" with her father and the same titled standards album.  Michael Feinstein, Harry Connick Jr, Michael Buble, Diana Krall, have all been re-inventors of the Amercian Songbook and out of our pop culture, we of the boomer generation have watched our icons, Keith Richards, Carly Simon, Joni Mitchell, Boz Skaggs, Robbie Williams, Sting, Pat Benatar, all working the canon in recent years.I've lent my ears to many of these, and I have to tell you, Harry Nilsson still tops the pops for me.  There just no comparable voice of interpretation to this album.  Unless you are a die-hard hard rocker, closed minded pop-eared musical minor with no appreciation for the craft of song, you will love this album.  I will not give a blow-by-blow analysis of the album, since there are reviews enough here to fill your bucket.  The bottom line is that A LITTLE TOUCH OF SCHMILSSON IN THE NIGHT is one of the best music investments anyone with an ear to our heritage in music can make.  His nuance and phrasing and interpretation are nothing short of stunning, emotional, and moving.  The arrangements and conducting by the giant of the genre, Gordon Jenkins is spectacular, and the engineering and now remastering of this album are supreme.  Bear in mind while listening to this magnificent work that the entire album was recorded in only 12 hours with no overdubs from engineering.  What you are hearing is a "live" recording, Harry singing with the orchestra as it all goes down on tape.  No added layers of vocals or strings and brass, it is the real deal as only Gordon Jenkins could have possibly accomplished, and a terrific nod to Derek Taylor, The Beatles publicist who brought Harry to their attention and sealed his fortune with public recognition; as this was Derek's first outing as a music producer and what a job he did!  This BMG release is the '88 revamp of the original which was released in the UK under the title "As Time Goes By" including the full BBC recording session that was filmed as it was being recorded.  The album was originally 12 tracks, now fully encompassing the entire recording of 19 tracks in the order they were meant to be enjoyed.  In the US it was release on CD as "A Touch More Schmilsson In The Night" using the same engineering and mastering as the UK release.  This CD is perfect to the "T".  Pour yourself a glass of fine wine, sit by the fireside, close your eyes and allow yourself to be transported to the bottom side of the 20th Century when you could identify a car by the grill or the fenders, and good movies were filmed in black and white and great movies in color were shown in theatres with huge elongated and rounded screens, and you could sit in the matinee all day if you wanted, watching shorts, double features, cartoons, and "lets all go to the lobby" commercials on one ticket to get in.This album truly is a little touch of Harry in the night.How To Buy A Harry Nilsson Album:(these are the best recommendations for CD to purchase, in sound quality and artist quality)(I will be posting reviews for all of them)Pandemonium Shadow Show, December 1967,Pandemonium Shadow Show, Aerial Ballet and Aerial Pandemonium BalletAerial Ballet, August 1968,Pandemonium Shadow Show, Aerial Ballet and Aerial Pandemonium BalletHarry, August 1969,Harry / Nilsson Sings NewmanNilsson Sings Newman, February 1970,Harry / Nilsson Sings NewmanThe Point, March 1971,The Point! Unlike its father, Son Of was a tale of eccentric bawdiness, crass humor, juvenile humor, and some may have even thought it a blunt stick. True Nilsson fans loved the hell out it, while fans of SCHMILSSON alone were soon to divorce themselves from the album, ergo it could be found in 2nd hand record shops easily, soon after its release. My, my, Harry, what have you done? Even some of his long time but more conservative fans, who followed him from the outset to The Point! and on the Schmilsson just couldn't find redemption in this one. Anyone with a brain in his head and eyes open to the nature of the beast can easily see that sometimes it is going to do what a beast does, it acts like a beast and follows its own natural bent. And Nilsson, no matter how much we guffaw about it, had a wickedly funny side to him that we only caught glimpses of before. So we bought our SON OF SCHMILSSON album, brought it home and plopped the platter on the turntable. "Take 54" is sung seriously out of tune by an alter ego of Harry Nilsson who is quite upset about his devolving relationship with the girl, who seems to ignore the recording studio door "with the red light on it". He sang his "balls off for you, baby" and how do you repay him? Well after that the song fades into the REM sleep of a snoring Richard Perry who awakens to creepy sound effects and a Hammer Horror voice shouting "Son of Schmilsson", etc. Imagine That! Well we can easily dismiss that one, besides, the 2nd song, "Remember" is a lovely, Christmas-ey, Harry Nilsson song that everyone loves. Yes it is radio friendly, has nice string arrangement and piano work, pretty vocals, a homey message, and we are on our way! To "Joy", a country-western parody that will have you holding your belly from achingly funny if you have never heard it before, it naturally segues, lyrically and musically into "Turn On Your Radio", another nice Nilsson tune that almost hearkens back to the early Nilsson days, okay we have one clunker so far, one pretty, one funny, and one reminiscing song. So the final song on side one of the record is coming. It's called "You're Breaking My Heart", aw this must be a tear-jerker, get your hankies out... So loud raucous rampaging horns accompanying Harry on vocals and electric piano, acoustic piano by Nicky Hopkins, Klaus Voorman on bass and sax, Peter Frampton on lead electric guitar and George Harrison on slide guitar, this is what you hear on You're Breaking My Heart. That...and the lyrics that accusingly alarm "You're breaking my heart, you're tearing it apart, so [expletive deleted] you!" Yes, Harry dropped the F-bomb in song, probably the first time on record since The Fish Cheer by Country Joe at Woodstock, and year earlier than Pink Floyd used the vulgar form of male cow excrement in "Money". How many teenagers were playing this record with the door open when Mom and Dad were within hailing distance? The way I figure it, Harry was going through that messy divorce thing at the time and this song probably just FELT really really good at the time ("I dunno, I was really drunk at the time..."). Turn the record over before Mom comes to the door, turn it up and you can't hear her knocking! Yeah that's the refrain that makes "Spaceman" such a terrific song! First of all, Elton beat Harry to the launching pad but Harry used better fuel and it's not burning out, he's just stuck spinning around the world and the bop vocal backing has so much more energy than that silly old "rocket man". Listen to them both now and tell me which one sounds "dated". `Sides, Ringo plays drums on this one!!! Okay, concession here, Elton's version is supposed to be dramatic, Harry's song is most definitely humorous, or at least anecdotal. "The Lottery Song" is cute little diddy about striking it rich and moving to Vegas to be famous. It has everything a cute little diddy should have, charm, wit, and greed. Ah! Here comes a reprise of "Remember", "long ago...far away...[burp!]...excuse me!" oh Harry yer jess so funny! But dig that rocking rhythm guitar and drums, Ringo on drums and Ray Cooper on congas, Frampton and Chris Spedding on dual lead guitars, Nicky Hopkins, Klaus again, and Bobby Keys on tenor sax, all rocking out to The El Dorados doo-wop Crazy Little Mama "At My Front Door"! and that one is followed by a slow building blues-rock "Ambush" which is very hard to decide if it is a serious anti-war thumping chant, or a tongue in cheek poke at something else, by now you are just so jaded, but it's a terrific song! And it is a great vocal exercise by Harry. Then Harry decided to go to a British old-folks home and whoop up a sing-a-long with the boys and girls, "I'd Rather Be Dead" ("than wet my bed"). Now THIS is humor! (actually it grows on you with age, almost 40 years later I can say I love it more today than when I used to skip it outright). So how does one end an album filled with redolent debauchery and obtuse jokes? In fact, you equate the World to a Girl and write a love song for "her", start it out in a quasi-island jibe with poor Caribbean Ricky Ricardo accent (be sure to include gargle and spit during the interlude), and then slow it down to an orchestrated love ballad ("I love the way you wear your trees") ending in a deeply efficacious line, "tell her she's beautiful, roll the world over, and give her a kiss...and a feel". Yes, yes! It's all in good fun, and when was the last time you listened to music and had good childish laugh? This is the Harry Nilsson who got bombed with John Lennon and together headed down to The Troubador to heckle The Smothers Brothers until they got thrown out! The cover must have given you SOME indication, I mean for Pete's Sake, Dracula? Okay, one of the worst bombs in movie history but great soundtrack! Most of the songs are from Schmilsson and Son Of Schmilsson, and it boasted one minor hit single itself, "Daybreak" which has finally found its way onto this album as a bonus track for the BMG remaster release. It sounds so much better than the poor quality recording that was used in some compilation albums. There are other bonus tracks to boost this romper room romp and add to the comedic frolick but the bottom line is this, serious now folks, SON OF SCHMILSSON was quite definitely for The Nilsson Fan and for the same public who got a kick out of Benny Hill and Monty Python, so if that is not your bag, then by all means, don't waste your money and skip this album. is meant to be for kicks and giggles but it has some real gems on it too. Remember, At My Front Door (the only non-Nilsson written song on the album), Ambush, and Spaceman being the more progressive ones and who cannot love the finale of "The Most Beautiful World In The World"? LOVE IT!!!A LITTLE TOUCH OF SCHMILSSON IN THE NIGHTBeholding him, plucks comfort from his looks:A largess universal like the sunHis liberal eye doth give to every one,Thawing cold fear, that mean and gentle all,Behold, as may unworthiness define,A little touch of Harry in the night.(William Shakespeare, Henry V, Act IV, Prologue)Henry the 5th, affectionately called "Harry" by his battle-weary troops, comforted his men in the field before the morning's charge against the enemy, "A little touch of Harry in the night", and these nocturnal visits is where Harry Nilsson derived the title for an album of music; from a pop-rock artist no less, in 1973 no less, from "The Great American Songbook". It was this concept which Harry had, to address the music of our pre-rock and roll, pre-modern era, songs of warmth and comfort, from the stalwarts of 20th century composition, and to tackle songs which require, by definition, the greatest of vocal acrobatics, and vocal beauty. Harry's voice, and this music, were a match made in heaven. This was, again, another step up, a very risky and very challenging task."The Great American Songbook" is a hypothetical construct that "seeks to represent the best American songs of the 20th century principally from Broadway theatre, musical theatre, and Hollywood musicals, from the 1920s to 1960, including dozens of songs of enduring popularity." (Alec Wilder)Mainly through the work of Alec Wilder, in 1972, after over a decade of research, he published what is now considered the "canon" of American Popular Song, beginning in 1900 and ending it in 1950 with the near advent of rock and roll. The Great American Songbook is essentially a ranking and study of composers and creative efforts. He identifies specifically Jerome Kern, Irving Berlin, George Gershwin, Richard Rodgers, Cole Porter, Harold Arlen, Vincent Youmans, Arthur Schwartz, Burton Lane, Hugh Martin, and Vernon Duke. Whiting, Ray Noble, John Green, Rube Bloom, and Jimmy Van Heusen. Lastly he concluded his research with a 67 page chapter of "Outstanding Individual Songs" which were singled out from the works of Harold Arlen, Irving Berlin, Nacio Herb Brown, Hoagy Carmichael, Walter Donaldson, Vernon Duke, Duke Ellington, Sammy Fain, George and Ira Gershwin, Ray Henderson, Herman Hupfeld, Bart Howard, Isham Jones, Jerome Kern, Frank Loesser, Jimmy McHugh, Johnny Mercer, Cole Porter, Rodgers and Hart, Rodgers and Hammerstein, Harry Ruby and Bert Kalmar, Arthur Schwartz and Howard Dietz, Jule Styne, Jimmy Van Heusen, Harry Warren, Richard Whiting, Jack Yellen, Vincent Youmans, and Victor Young.There is a style and a structure which is categorically definable to all of the song craft in the songbook, from the composers above, but that would require a musicology degree and more technical proficiency than this writer has. I can, however, with complete confidence, identify A LITTLE TOUCH OF SCHMILSSON IN THE NIGHT as a singular supreme effort which perfectly resonates with that style and structure which makes the songs he worked from the lists above something more than total enlightenment.There has been a recent revival of The Great American Songbook in the last two decades, especially since Rod Stewart began his gravelly crooning (which answers the question, exactly just how many American Songbook albums can someone make?) Actually, believe it or not, it began in 1970 with Ringo Starr's Sentimental Journey album, his first after the breakup of The Beatles. It was critically praised but not a terrific seller on the market. Harry was next in 1973 with this album. Michael Feinstein, Harry Connick Jr, Michael Buble, Diana Krall, have all been re-inventors of the Amercian Songbook and out of our pop culture, we of the boomer generation have watched our icons, Keith Richards, Carly Simon, Joni Mitchell, Boz Skaggs, Robbie Williams, Sting, Pat Benatar, all working the canon in recent years.I've lent my ears to many of these, and I have to tell you, Harry Nilsson still tops the pops for me. There just no comparable voice of interpretation to this album. Unless you are a die-hard hard rocker, closed minded pop-eared musical minor with no appreciation for the craft of song, you will love this album. The bottom line is that A LITTLE TOUCH OF SCHMILSSON IN THE NIGHT is one of the best music investments anyone with an ear to our heritage in music can make. His nuance and phrasing and interpretation are nothing short of stunning, emotional, and moving. Bear in mind while listening to this magnificent work that the entire album was recorded in only 12 hours with no overdubs from engineering. What you are hearing is a "live" recording, Harry singing with the orchestra as it all goes down on tape. No added layers of vocals or strings and brass, it is the real deal as only Gordon Jenkins could have possibly accomplished, and a terrific nod to Derek Taylor, The Beatles publicist who brought Harry to their attention and sealed his fortune with public recognition; as this was Derek's first outing as a music producer and what a job he did! This BMG release is the '88 revamp of the original which was released in the UK under the title "As Time Goes By" including the full BBC recording session that was filmed as it was being recorded. This CD is perfect to the "T". Pour yourself a glass of fine wine, sit by the fireside, close your eyes and allow yourself to be transported to the bottom side of the 20th Century when you could identify a car by the grill or the fenders, and good movies were filmed in black and white and great movies in color were shown in theatres with huge elongated and rounded screens, and you could sit in the matinee all day if you wanted, watching shorts, double features, cartoons, and "lets all go to the lobby" commercials on one ticket to get in.This album truly is a little touch of Harry in the night.How To Buy A Harry Nilsson Album:(these are the best recommendations for CD to purchase, in sound quality and artist quality)(I will be posting reviews for all of them)Pandemonium Shadow Show, December 1967,Pandemonium Shadow Show, Aerial Ballet and Aerial Pandemonium BalletAerial Ballet, August 1968,Pandemonium Shadow Show, Aerial Ballet and Aerial Pandemonium BalletHarry, August 1969,Harry / Nilsson Sings NewmanNilsson Sings Newman, February 1970,Harry / Nilsson Sings NewmanThe Point, March 1971,The Point! reviewText: This is another masterpiece from the Isleys, this album is life itself!!. From matters of the heart to the challenges of humanity,this album is SOLID!!.Check out songs like "harvest for the world" and "people of today", they are a direct wake up call to us all, then the praising, "at your best you are love" so flowing and mellow,  then the greiving and painful,"let me down easy" , sad and beautiful at the same time!!. Topping off this great effort is two more bouncy pieces, "so you wanna stay down" and "you still feel the need". A bonus live recording of "summer breeze" is included here as well. As long as life last, and civilisation is intact, this album will endure. I recomend this one to all who love strong, effective music, fan of the Isleys or otherwise. It is a worthy addition to any music collection!!!.
summary: A TRUE HARVEST OF LIFE AND LOVE!!

reviewText: This is a weak effort.  Sure her lyrics are pretty good (hence the second star) but the high school talent show guitar playing and her countryish voice are not getting it done.  I couldn't pay attention to one song long  enough to remember it.  While riding in the car trying to listen to this my  mind wandered everywhere and I looked doen and thought, track 12, already?  I know that this makes some of you psuedo-intellectuals feel  "smart" when you listen to it, but I suggest you take a course in  Differential Equations for that.  I love "Who Will Save Your  Soul", and wait for an album that sounds like that song, but until  then I'm going to pick on my wife for buying this for me for Christmas (I  could have gotten the Partridge Family's Greatest Hits cheaper).

reviewText: This collection includes a wide range of Cher's commercial hits, focusing on the Geffen recordings (1987 - 1991): "If I Could Turn Back Time," "I Found Someone," "Love and Understanding," etc.  There is also a good sampling of her Kapp and MCA Records (early 1970s) hits: "The Way of Love," "Dark Lady," "Gypsys, Tramps and Thieves," etc.  There's even the original "I Got You Babe" with Sonny.Of course, given Cher's prolific output, there's a lot missing.  Her early solo hits are missing and she had a considerable run of chart hits on Imperial Records in the 1960s.  If you stop to think about it, Cher is a phenomenon.  She's been a successful performer and recording artist for 40 years!!!  That she is more successful today than ever before proves that there is some justice in the world.So, this collection is not definitive, but it is fun.  And that is worth five stars in itself.

reviewText: The Notorious B.I.G.'s debut album is one of the few hip hop albums that can be considered timeless.  While it didn't sell as much as the massive Life Ater Death (which is a classic to its credit), it is a much better album.There are so many classic songs and quotes throughout this amazing album to even name.  Doing a track by track review of the album would be pointless, since every song can only be described in one word: unbelievable.  What makes this album so great is how it blends some of the best street tales ever with phenomenal party songs.  This is what makes Biggie the best MC ever; his uncanny ability to make classic albums that appeal to the masses.  The only rapper that can come close to him in that category is 2Pac.In the end, Ready To Die is placed in the same category as Illmatic, 36 Chambers, and Cuban Linx as the best revolutionary debut albums ever in hip hop.  Along with Life After Death, it is the blueprint for what hip hop albums are today: mix some street songs with party songs and you'll have a successful album.  Unfortunately nobody has ever been able to match any of Biggie's albums in that respect.
summary: One of the best hip hop albums ever

reviewText: This was the second album I bought by the incredible Soft Machine (got Third first)and it's a great one. Although many American ensembles get all the credit for great jazz-rock fusion, Soft Machine, along with fellow countrymen Henry Cow deserve a nod as well. For some reason I find this to be a great night time driving album, and my cassette copy finds it's way into my car very often. I would actually recommend this as an intro to the band over the more highly regarded Third, mostly because the pieces are a little shorter and it's a single album.Soft Machine's music can be quite demanding of the listener and a shorter first dose may sit better with the uninitiated listener.

reviewText: Into the Fire was a very strong album on its own!  Although it had to compete with U2's album in the spring of 1987, it had a good string of hits.  That In the Heat of the Night is still a rocker to this day.  But one of the album's big surprises is Another Day and its fast moving paces and bridges that is done so remarkably in 3 minutes and 40 seconds!  Victim of Love is still a solid ballad.  One of the more dramatic performances on here is Remembrance Day. History dramatically sung by Bryan in some 6 minutes.  For Bryan to follow a very mega successful album in Reckless from '84 is a hard feat.  But Into The Fire did well on its own strength.  It helped make Bryan a more acceptable artist and songwriter.

reviewText: Cam'ron released his 1st CD in 1998 called "Confessions Of Fire".  The CD was pretty good with a mixture of street and commercial songs.  His first single "357" sampled the theme from the TV show "Magnum PI" and was a very catchy tune.  What got Cam'ron noticed the most, however, was a song featuring his Harlem partner in crime, Mase, called "Horse And Carriage".  This Trackmasters' produced tune was an instant hit and while Cam'ron was known for his mixed tape appearances and street rhymes, he started becoming mainstream after "Horse And Carriage" was in heavy radio rotation.  On his 2000 release "S.D.E." it seemed as if Cam'ron was going for a different approach.  While songs on his debut featured songs with Usher, Kelly Price, and the late Kenny Greene of Intro, on "S.D.E." it seemed as if Cam'ron was trying to take things back to the streets.  However, "S.D.E." ended up doing the same thing as his debut CD did after his 1st single "What Means The World To Me" was released to radio.  While the CD was street oriented, it became known for his 1st single and the song with Destiny's Child "Do It Again".  Cam'ron had memorable street anthems on both of his CDs with songs like "Glory" w/Noreaga, "D Rugs", "Losin' Weight" w/Prodigy of Mobb Deep, "Where I'm From" w/Dutch & Spade and "Double Up" w/Juelz.  The song "Pull It" w/DMX, which was another mixtape favorite, never made it to his debut CD because the sample wouldn't clear.  After his first two CDs on Epic, Cam'ron signed with the infamous Rocafella records and many people thought that this move would automatically put him at another level.  However, although there are some certified bangers on his 3rd disc, "Come Home With Me".  There is not much difference between his debut CD and his new one.  First of all, Cam'ron completed most of the CD before he went to Rocafella Records and some of the material definitely displays this.  The hit of this CD and the first single is clearly "Oh Boy".  Cam'ron and Juelz Santana tear this Just Blaze track to shreds.  It does not get better than this on the CD and fans of Cam'ron's other 2 discs will see what I am seeing.  From there, you get a track featuring Cam'ron and Jay Z called "Welcome To New York City" and Juelz Santana is featured on the chorus.  This song is "straight fire" as some would say.  The two go back and forth about "The home of 9/11, the place of the lost towers" and "the birthplace of Michael Jordan and the home of Biggie Smalls".  Once again, Just Blaze provides the beat and everything is fine from there.  On "The ROC (Just Fire)", Memphis Bleek and Beanie Sigel, join Cam'ron on which will definitely be remembered as a Rocafella classic.  Memphis Bleek once again displays his potential, he just fails to deliver on his own CDs.  The problem with "Come Home With Me" lie within the artist and the choice of samples.  There is entirely too much sampling going on here.  It seems they are trying to balance Killa Cam and the commercial side of things as well and at times this does not work.  There are some catchy commercial tunes such as "Hey Ma", which uses the Commodores' "Easy (Like Sunday Morning)" sample and "On Fire Tonight" which uses Mtume's "You, Me & He" sample.  "Daydreaming" takes the chorus straight from Aretha Franklin and may grow on you after a few listens.  "Losing Weight Part 2" w/Juelz Santana is a pretty good song but the track is nothing like the original version with Prodigy.  However, I don't think a sequel with Prodigy was ever considered, so you can't blame Cam'ron.  If you can get past the commercial missteps on some songs then this is a pretty good CD.  Other noteworthy songs include "Life My Life (Leave Me Alone" w/Daz which uses the same beat as 2 Pac used on "Ambitionz Of A Ridah", the title track w/Juelz Santana and Jimmy Jones that deals with the harsh realities of life, "Dead Or Alive" w/Jimmy Jones, "I Just Wanna" w/Juelz Santana and the mixtape favorite "Boy Boy".  Overall, some Cam'ron fans will want to listen to his 1st two discs and leave this one alone.  However, I feel that "Come Home With Me" is worth checking out if you are a true Cam'ron fan.  He shows some growth and he also sticks to the same formula as "Confessions Of Fire".  The next time around, however, I would just say more Just Blaze and Kanye West and less commercial samples.James' Top 51) Oh Boy w/Juelz Santana2) Welcome To New York City w/Jay Z & Juelz Santana3) The ROC (Just Fire) w/Memphis Bleek & Beanie Sigel4) Live My Life (Leave Me Alone) w/Daz5) Losing Weight Part 2 w/Juelz Santana
summary: Cam'ron, as presented by The ROC

On tracks like "Make Me Believe," he makes the tracks his with beautiful singing during the breakdown, and elsewhere - the Awake-ish "I Am" and the peaceful "Serenity" - he shows that his vocals are not to be underestimated. If you want to hear Sully both shriek to great effect - "Changes" and "I F****** Hate You" - and belt out great harmonies/melodies, then pick this one up.

reviewText: Joni begins her jazz journey, with a much denser layer of production.  Tom Scott and the LA Express fill the grooves with lush winds. She gets  assistance from another Canadian great, Robbie Robertson, on probably her most rocking tune, "Raised on Robbery".  The engineering production on that tune grabs the listener immediately.  The disk is brilliant from cover to cover, including the airplay hits, "Court and Spark", "Help Me", "Free Man in Paris", through the remake of the "Crazy", with guest vocals by Cheech and Chong.  I love this disk, and I recommend it highly.  Joni's guitar tunings are set to showcase the strength of her vocal range, and her piano is lovely as well.

reviewText: Put the O Back in Country is a great debut album from Shooter Jennings that sounds nothing like anything that has come out of Nashville in recent years.  It's rough and unpolished and at will probably never be played on the radio.  It is just the kind of album that country music has been missing for a long time.Shooter may be the guy to put life back into the outlaw movement started many years ago by the likes of Johnny Cash and, of course, Waylon.  And while there will no doubt be comparisons between Shooter and his father, he does not sound like and doesn't try to sound like his father.  But like his predecessors, his music is against the grain and raw and will hopefully have the same kind of lasting effect on the music industry.As far as the cd, the weakest song, by far, is the title track, with my favorites being 4th of July, which sounds a lot like early Steve Earle, Manifesto #1 and Southern Comfort.  All of the songs are solid and are well worth the money, which is a rare accomplishment for a country artist these days.

reviewText: From the first notes of `The Right Thing Right' you know Johnny Marr means business. It's a cross between The Jam jangle, Ian McCulloch vocal prowess, and that driving rhythm that pushed so many of The Smiths great songs(there were many). There's even a touch of Cheap Trick bombast that starts the song out. You listen to this opening track and wonder why it took Marr so long to put out a proper solo release.  Sure, he had Johnny Marr and the Healers back in 2003. But he was still under the protective umbrella of a band. For the first time in over a 20 year career Johnny Marr is on his own, without the watchful eye of old lady Morrissey or countless other bands that were fortunate enough to have Johnny Marr sling guitar in their bands and ultimately make them more important and better than they actually were. Is The Messenger a game changer? It depends on what rule book you're playing from. Either way, it's a great album to get lost in for a little under an hour.I often wondered how Johnny Marr lasted as long as he did with Morrissey. I mean sure, The Smiths were amazing, and Morrissey had a big part in that. But without Johnny Marr's musical magic it would've been nothing more than Stephen Morrissey's Oscar Wilde impressions. Johnny Marr provided the lush musical pages onto which Morrissey could write his scathing verbiage. There might not be the stories of naught Headmasters and girlfriends in comas, but the drama is still retained in Marr's knack for great melody play. On The Messenger Marr seems to be making up for lost time, as the musical scope ranges from Smiths-ian drama to punchy power pop to straight up rock `n roll. `I Want The Heartbeat' and `European Me' are great and dramatic tracks that could've sat nicely on an Smiths album. Then `Upstarts' comes in and punches you in the gut with a hook that grabs you and never lets go. This is the kind of track the brothers Gallagher wish they could've written back in the mid-90s. So much has been said about the Beatles fetish Oasis held, and indeed there was plenty of Fab Four borrowing going on.  But I think there was just as much of a love for The Smiths, and in particular Johnny Marr's knack for writing grandiose pop music while retaining an angry punk spirit underneath all the shimmer. Title track `The Messenger' has a dance-y sway to it, with a DFA-approved bass line and a wonderful guitar hook. Johnny Marr also has a particularly great voice, which also makes me wonder why he's played second fiddle for so long. He should've been front and center since 1988. `Generate! Generate!' is a great bouncer of a track that Art Brut and Franz Ferdinand have been trying to write since 2004. `Word Starts Attack' ends the album as the death knell for bands like Franz Ferdinand, Kaiser Chiefs, Art Brut, and the like. We appreciate you all filling in for as long as did, but we don't need you anymore.I've heard it said that this album should've come out back in the early 90s, and truth be told, it does carry the spirit and sound of that era. But you can't argue with a good song, and a track like `New Town Velocity' defies eras and time frames. It's a great song, regardless of the era it was created. That sentiment sums up The Messenger. It's a great album, despite coming out a decade or two late. Johnny Marr is finally front and center, right where he should be.
